I have heard the Buddha say that to know all phenomena are empty and to realize the nature of all phenomena is to behold the Dharma-body with the eye of wisdom." At that time, the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā, wishing to be the first to see the Buddha, transformed herself into a wheel-turning king, guided by the seven treasures and guarded by the fourfold army, and upon arriving at the place of the World-Honored One, she returned to her form as a bhikṣuṇī. The Tathāgata replied, "You are not the first to see me. Shanxian (Subhūti), contemplating the emptiness of all phenomena — it is he who has seen the Dharma-body." Within the enclosure of the sacred traces, miraculous signs occurred one after another. To the southeast of the great stūpa, there is a dragon pond, and the dragon constantly protects the sacred traces. Because there is this unseen protection, they are difficult to violate lightly; though they have decayed naturally over the long years, no person has been able to destroy them. Traveling southeast from here for less than two hundred li, one arrives at the country of Kanyakubja (羯若鞠闍國) (in the language of Tang, the Kingdom of the Hunchbacked Maiden City; it is within the borders of Central India).

zh: 羯若鞠闍國，周四千餘里。國大都城西臨殑伽河，其長二十餘里，廣四五里。城隍堅峻，臺閣相望，花林池沼，光鮮澄鏡。異方奇貨，多聚於此。居人豐樂，家室富饒。華菓具繁，稼穡時播。氣序和洽，風俗淳質。容貌妍雅，服飾鮮綺。篤學遊藝，談論清遠。邪正二道，信者相半。伽藍百餘所，僧徒萬餘人，大小二乘，兼功習學。天祠二百餘所，異道數千餘人。羯若鞠闍國人長壽時，其舊王城號拘蘇磨補羅（唐言花宮）。王號梵授，福智宿資，文武允備，威懾贍部，聲震隣國。具足千子，智勇弘毅，復有百女，儀貌妍雅。時有仙人居殑伽河側，棲神入定，經數萬歲，形如枯木，遊禽棲集，遺尼拘律果於仙人肩上，暑往寒來，垂蔭合拱。多歷年所，從定而起，欲去其樹，恐覆鳥巢，時人美其德，號大樹仙人。仙人寓目河濱，遊觀林薄，見王諸女相從嬉戲，欲界愛起，染著心生，便詣華宮，欲事禮請。王聞仙至，躬迎慰曰：「大仙棲情物外，何能輕舉？」仙人曰：「我棲林藪，彌積歲時，出定遊覽，見王諸女，染愛心生，自遠來請。」王聞其辭，計無所出，謂仙人曰：「今還所止，請俟嘉辰。」仙人聞命，遂還林藪。王乃歷問諸女，無肯應娉。王懼仙威，憂愁毀悴。其幼稚女候王事隙，從容問曰：「父王千子具足，萬國慕化，何故憂愁，如有所懼？」王曰：「大樹仙人幸顧求婚，而汝曹輩莫肯從命。仙有威力，能作災祥，儻不遂心，必起瞋怒，毀國滅祀，辱及先王。深惟此禍，誠有所懼。」稚女謝曰：「遺此深憂，我曹罪也。願以微軀，得延國祚。」王聞喜悅，命駕送歸。既至仙廬，謝仙人曰：「大仙俯方外之情，垂世間之顧，敢奉稚女，以供灑掃。」仙人見而不悅，乃謂王曰：「輕吾老叟，配此不妍。」王曰：「歷問諸女，無肯從命。唯此幼稚，願充給使。」仙人懷怒，便惡呪曰：「九十九女，一時腰曲，形既毀弊，畢世無婚。」王使往驗，果已背傴。從是之後，便名曲女城焉。今王，本吠奢種也，字曷利沙伐彈那（唐言喜增）。君臨有土，二世三王。父字波羅羯羅伐彈那（唐言作光增），兄字曷邏闍伐彈那（唐言王增）。王增以長嗣位，以德治政。時東印度羯羅拏蘇伐剌那（唐言金耳）國設賞迦王（唐言月），每謂臣曰：「隣有賢主，國之禍也。」於是誘請，會而害之。人既失君，國亦荒亂。時大臣婆尼（唐言辯了），職望隆重，謂僚庶曰：「國之大計，定於今日。先王之子，亡君之弟，仁慈天性，孝敬因心，親賢允屬，欲以襲位。於事何如？各言爾志。」眾咸仰德，嘗無異謀。於是輔臣執事咸勸進曰：「王子垂聽，先王積功累德，光有國祚。嗣及王增，謂終壽考；輔佐無良，棄身讎手，為國大恥，下臣罪也。物議時謠，允歸明德。光臨土宇，克復親讎，雪國之恥，光父之業，功孰大焉？幸無辭矣！」王子曰：「國嗣之重，今古為難，君人之位，興立宜審。我誠寡德，父兄遐棄，推襲大位，其能濟乎？物議為宜，敢忘虛薄？今者殑伽河岸，有觀自在菩薩像，既多靈鑒，願往請辭。」即至菩薩像前，斷食祈請。菩薩感其誠心，現形問曰：「爾何所求，若此勤懇？」王子曰：「我惟積禍，慈父云亡；重茲酷罰，仁兄見害。自顧寡德，國人推尊，令襲大位，光父之業。愚昧無知，敢希聖旨！」菩薩告曰：「汝於先身，在此林中為練若苾芻，而精勤不懈。承茲福力，為此王子。金耳國王既毀佛法，爾紹王位，宜重興隆，慈悲為志，傷愍居懷，不久當王五印度境。欲延國祚，當從我誨，冥加景福，隣無強敵。勿昇師子之座，勿稱大王之號。」於是受教而退，即襲王位，自稱曰王子，號尸羅阿迭多（唐言戒日）。於是謂臣曰：「兄讎未報，隣國不賓，終無右手進食之期。凡爾庶僚，同心勠力。」遂總率國兵，講習戰士。象軍五千，馬軍二萬，步軍五萬，自西徂東，征伐不臣。象不解鞍，人不釋甲，於六年中，臣五印度。既廣其地，更增甲兵。象軍六萬，馬軍十萬。垂三十年，兵戈不起，政教和平，務修節儉，營福樹善，忘寢與食。令五印度不得噉肉，若斷生命，有誅無赦。於殑伽河側建立數千窣堵波，各高百餘尺。於五印度城邑、鄉聚、達巷、交衢，建立精廬，儲飲食，止醫藥，施諸羈貧，周給不殆。聖迹之所，並建伽藍。五歲一設無遮大會，傾竭府庫，惠施群有，唯留兵器，不充檀捨。歲一集會諸國沙門，於三七日中，以四事供養，莊嚴法座，廣飾義筵，令相摧論，校其優劣，褒貶淑慝，黜陟幽明。若戒行貞固，道德淳邃，推昇師子之座，王親受法；戒雖清淨，學無稽古，但加敬禮，示有尊崇；律儀無紀，穢德已彰，驅出國境，不願聞見。隣國小王、輔佐大臣，殖福無殆，求善忘勞，即携手同座，謂之善友；其異於此，面不對辭，事有聞議，通使往復。而巡方省俗，不常其居，隨所至止，結廬而舍。唯雨三月，多雨不行。每於行宮日修珍饌，飯諸異學，僧眾一千，婆羅門五百。每以一日分作三時，一時理務治政，二時營福修善，孜孜不倦，竭日不足矣。初，受拘摩羅王請曰，自摩揭陀國往迦摩縷波國。時戒日王巡方在羯朱嗢祇羅國，命拘摩羅王曰：「宜與那爛陀遠客沙門速來赴會。」於是遂與拘摩羅王往會見焉。戒日王勞苦已曰：「自何國來，將何所欲？」對曰：「從大唐國來，請求佛法。」王曰：「大唐國在何方？經途所亘，去斯遠近？」對曰：「當此東北數萬餘里，印度所謂摩訶至那國是也。」王曰：「嘗聞摩訶至那國有秦王天子，少而靈鑒，長而神武。昔先代喪亂，率土分崩，兵戈競起，群生荼毒，而秦王天子早懷遠略，興大慈悲，拯濟含識，平定海內，風教遐被，德澤遠洽，殊方異域，慕化稱臣。民庶荷其亭育，咸歌《秦王破陣樂》。聞其雅頌，于茲久矣。盛德之譽，誠有之乎？大唐國者，豈此是耶？」對曰：「然。至那者，前王之國號；大唐者，我君之國稱。昔未襲位，謂之秦王；今已承統，稱曰天子。前代運終，群生無主，兵戈亂起，殘害生靈。秦王天縱含弘，心發慈愍，威風鼓扇，群凶殄滅，八方靜謐，萬國朝貢。愛育四生，敬崇三寶，薄賦斂，省刑罰，而國用有餘，氓俗無穴，風猷大化，難以備舉。」戒日王曰：「盛哉！彼土群生，福感聖主。」時戒日王將還曲女城設法會也，從數十萬眾，在殑伽河南岸。拘摩羅王從數萬之眾，居北岸。分河中流，水陸並進。二王導引，四兵嚴衛，或泛舟，或乘象，擊鼓鳴螺，拊弦奏管。經九十日，至曲女城，在殑伽河西大花林中。是時諸國二十餘王，先奉告命，各與其國髦俊沙門及婆羅門、群官、兵士，來集大會。王先於河西建大伽藍；伽藍東起寶臺，高百餘尺，中有金佛像，量等王身；臺南起寶壇，為浴佛像之處；從此東北十四五里，別築行宮。是時，仲春月也。從初一日，以珍味饌諸沙門、婆羅門，至二十一日。自行宮屬伽藍，夾道為閣，窮諸瑩飾，樂人不移，雅聲遞奏。王於行宮出一金像，虛中隱起，高餘三尺，載以大象，張以寶幰。戒日王為帝釋之服，執寶蓋以左侍，拘摩羅王作梵王之儀，執白拂而右侍。各五百象軍，被鎧周衛，佛像前後各百大象，樂人以乘，鼓奏音樂。戒日王以真珠雜寶及金銀諸花，隨步四散，供養三寶。先就寶壇，香水浴像，王躬負荷，送上西臺，以諸珍寶、憍奢耶衣數十百千，而為供養。是時唯有沙門二十餘人預從，諸國王為侍衛。饌食已訖，集諸異學，商確微言，抑揚至理。日將曛暮，迴駕行宮。如是日送金像，導從如初，以至散日。其大臺忽然火起，伽藍門樓煙焰方熾。王曰：「罄捨國珍，奉為先王，建此伽藍，式昭勝業，寡德無祐，有斯災異，咎徵若此，何用生為！」乃焚香禮請而自誓曰：「幸以宿善，王諸印度，願我福力，禳滅火災，若無所感，從此喪命！」尋即奮身，跳履門閫，若有撲滅，火盡煙消。諸王覩異，重增祇懼。已而顏色不動，辭語如故，問諸王曰：「忽此災變，焚燼成功，心之所懷，意將何謂？」諸王俯伏悲泣，對曰：「成功勝迹，冀傳來葉，一旦灰燼，何可為懷？況諸外道，快心相賀！」王曰：「以此觀之，如來所說誠也。外道異學守執常見，唯我大師無常是誨。然我檀捨已周，心願諧遂，屬斯變滅，重知如來誠諦之說，斯為大善，無可深悲。」於是從諸王東上大窣堵波，登臨觀覽。方下階陛，忽有異人持刃逆王，王時窘迫，却行進級，俯執此人，以付群官。是時群官惶遽，不知進救。諸王咸請誅戮此人，戒日王殊無忿色，止令不殺。王親問曰：「我何負汝，為此暴惡？」對曰：「大王德澤無私，中外荷負。然我狂愚，不謀大計，受諸外道一言之感，輒為刺客，首圖逆害。」王曰：「外道何故興此惡心？」對曰：「大王集諸國，傾府庫，供養沙門，鎔鑄佛像，而諸外道自遠召集，不蒙省問，心誠愧恥。乃令狂愚，敢行凶詐。」於是究問外道徒屬。有五百婆羅門，並諸高才，應命召集，嫉諸沙門蒙王禮重，乃射火箭，焚燒寶臺，冀因救火，眾人潰亂，欲以此時殺害大王，既無緣隙，遂雇此人，趨隘行刺。是時諸王、大臣請誅外道，王乃罰其首惡，餘黨不罪，遷五百婆羅門出印度之境。於是乃還都也。城西北窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。如來在昔，於此七日說諸妙法。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。復有如來髮、爪小窣堵波。說法窣堵波南，臨殑伽河，有三伽藍，同垣異門，佛像嚴麗，僧徒肅穆，役使淨人數千餘戶。精舍寶函中有佛牙，長餘寸半，殊光異色，朝變夕改。遠近相趨，士庶咸集，式修瞻仰，日百千眾。監守者繁其諠雜，權立重稅，宣告遠近：欲見佛牙，輸大金錢。然而瞻禮之徒，寔繁其侶，金錢之稅，悅以心競。每於齋日，出置高座，數百千眾，燒香散華，華雖盈積，牙函不沒。伽藍前左、右各有精舍，高百餘尺，石基塼室，其中佛像，眾寶莊飾，或鑄金、銀，或鎔鍮石。二精舍前各有小伽藍。伽藍東南不遠，有大精舍，石基塼室，高二百餘尺，中作如來立像，高三十餘尺，鑄以鍮石，飾諸妙寶。精舍四周石壁之上，雕畫如來修菩薩行所經事迹，備盡鐫鏤。石精舍南不遠，有日天祠。祠南不遠，有大自在天祠。並瑩青石，俱窮雕刻，規摹度量，同佛精舍。各有千戶充其灑掃，鼓樂絃歌晝夜無徙。大城東南六七里，殑伽河南，有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。在昔如來於此六月說身無常、苦、空、不淨。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。又有如來髮、爪小窣堵波，人有染疾，至誠旋繞，必得痊愈，蒙其福利。
en_current: The country of Kanyākubja (羯若鞠闍國) is over four thousand li in circumference. The capital city borders the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) to the west; it is over twenty li in length and four to five li in breadth. The city moats and ramparts are solid and steep, with towers and pavilions facing one another, and flower groves and ponds that are bright and clear as mirrors. Rare goods from distant regions are mostly gathered here. The inhabitants are prosperous and happy, and their households are wealthy and abundant. Flowers and fruits are plentiful, and crops are sown in their proper seasons. The climate is harmonious and mild, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are refined in appearance and wear bright and elegant clothing. They are devoted to learning and skilled in the arts, and their discourse is clear and profound. Regarding the two paths of the heterodox and the orthodox, the number of believers is about equal. There are over one hundred saṅghārāmas and more than ten thousand monks, who study both the Great and Small Vehicles with equal diligence. There are over two hundred deva temples, and several thousand followers of heterodox paths.  In the age when the people of the country of Kanyākubja enjoyed long lives, the old capital city was called Kusumapura (拘蘇磨補羅) (In the language of the Tang, this means "Flowery Palace"). The king was named Brahmadatta (梵授); he possessed the accumulated merits of wisdom and virtue, was fully accomplished in both civil and military affairs, his power intimidated Jambudvīpa, and his fame shook neighboring countries. He had a full thousand sons, who were wise, brave, magnanimous, and resolute; he also had one hundred daughters, who were beautiful in appearance and refined in manner.  At that time, there was a rishi living by the side of the Gaṅgā who concentrated his spirit in meditative absorption for tens of thousands of years until his form resembled a withered tree. Migratory birds perched and gathered there, dropping a nyagrodha fruit upon the rishi's shoulder; as summers went and winters came, it cast a shade and grew to the size of an arch. After many years had passed, he rose from his meditation and wished to remove the tree, but fearing he might overturn the birds' nests, he desisted. The people of the time praised his virtue and called him the "Rishi of the Big Tree." The rishi cast his eyes along the riverbank and wandered through the thickets, where he saw the king’s daughters playing together. Desire for the world of the senses arose, and a heart of attachment was born; he then went to the magnificent palace, wishing to make a formal request. When the king heard the rishi had arrived, he went to welcome him in person and greeted him, saying, "The great rishi dwells in spirit beyond the material world; what has prompted this sudden visit?" The rishi said, "I have dwelt in the forest and marshes for many years. Emerging from meditation to wander, I saw the king’s daughters, and a heart of attachment was born; I have come from afar to make a request." Hearing these words, the king was at a loss for a plan and said to the rishi, "Return now to your dwelling; please wait for an auspicious day." The rishi heard this command and returned to the forest and marshes. The king then asked each of his daughters in turn, but none would consent to the marriage. Fearing the rishi’s power, the king became sorrowful and haggard. His youngest daughter, waiting for a break in the king’s affairs, calmly asked, "Father, you have a full thousand sons and ten thousand nations admire your transformation; for what reason are you so sorrowful, as if you are in fear?" The king said, "The Rishi of the Big Tree (Mahāvṛkṣa-ṛṣi) has deigned to seek a marriage alliance, yet none of you sisters are willing to obey. An immortal possesses great power and can bring about either disaster or fortune; if his heart’s desire is not met, he will surely fall into a rage, destroying the kingdom, ending our ancestral sacrifices, and bringing shame upon the late kings. Deeply contemplating this calamity, I am truly afraid." The youngest daughter replied, "To have caused this deep sorrow is our fault. I am willing to offer my humble self to preserve the prosperity of the state." Hearing this, the king was overjoyed; he ordered a carriage to be prepared and sent her to him. Upon arriving at the hermit’s hut, the king thanked the hermit, saying, "The great hermit has condescended from his transcendent state to show concern for worldly affairs; I dare to offer my young daughter to serve you by sweeping and cleaning." The hermit saw her and was displeased, saying to the king, "You slight this old man by matching me with one so unattractive." The king replied, "I have asked all my daughters, and none were willing to obey. Only this young one is willing to serve as a maid." The hermit, harboring anger, uttered a wicked curse: "May the ninety-nine daughters all have their waists bent at once; their forms being thus ruined and spoiled, they shall have no marriage for their entire lives." The king sent someone to verify this, and indeed, their backs were already hunched. From that time on, it has been called the City of the Hunchbacked Maidens (Kanyakubja).  The present king is of the Vaiśya caste, and his name is Harṣavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Happiness"). He rules over the land, the third king of two generations. His father’s name was Prabhākaravardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of Light"), and his elder brother’s name was Rājyavardhana (translated into Chinese as "Increment of the Kingdom"). Rājyavardhana succeeded to the throne as the eldest and governed with virtue. At that time, King Śaśāṅka (translated into Chinese as "Moon") of the kingdom of Karṇasuvarṇa (translated into Chinese as "Golden Ear") in East India often said to his ministers, "To have a virtuous ruler in a neighboring state is a misfortune for one's own country." Thereupon, he lured and invited him, and at the meeting, he killed him. Once the people had lost their ruler, the country fell into chaos. At that time, the high minister Bhaṇi (translated into Chinese as "Eloquent and Wise"), whose position and reputation were of great weight, said to the officials and the populace, "The great plan for the country must be decided this day." "The son of the former king and younger brother of the deceased monarch is benevolent by nature and filial by heart; he is truly close to the virtuous, and I wish for him to succeed to the throne. What do you think of this matter? Each of you, speak your mind." The assembly all looked up to his virtue, and there was never any dissenting opinion. Thereupon, the assistant ministers and officials all exhorted him to take the throne, saying: "May the prince listen to us; the late king accumulated merits and cultivated virtues, gloriously possessing the mandate of the state. The succession reached Rājyavardhana, and we expected him to live out his full span of years; but his assistants were not good, and he abandoned his life at the hands of an enemy—this is a great shame for the country and the fault of us, your humble servants. Public opinion and the rumors of the time truly point to your brilliant virtue. If you were to grace the land and the territory, avenge your kin upon the enemy, wash away the shame of the country, and glorify the legacy of your father, what merit could be greater than this? We hope you will not decline!"  The prince said, "The matter of national succession has been a difficult one from ancient times to the present; the establishment of one in the position of a sovereign must be considered with great prudence. I am truly lacking in virtue, and now that my father and elder brother have been taken from me, if I were to be pushed to succeed to the great throne, would I be able to succeed in my duties? Although public opinion deems it appropriate, how could I forget my own insignificance? Now, on the bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) river, there is an image of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara (觀自在菩薩) which is highly responsive; I wish to go there to seek guidance."   He immediately went before the Bodhisattva's image and fasted to make his request. The Bodhisattva, moved by his sincerity, manifested his form and asked, "What do you seek, that you are so diligent and earnest?" The prince said, "I have only accumulated disasters; my benevolent father has passed away, and to add to this cruel punishment, my virtuous elder brother has been murdered. Reflecting on myself, I am lacking in virtue, yet the people of the country honor me and urge me to succeed to the great throne to glorify my father's legacy." "I am foolish and ignorant; how dare I hope for the holy decree!" The Bodhisattva replied, "In your former life, you were an āraṇyaka-bhikṣu (練若苾芻) in this forest, and you were diligent and unremitting. By the power of that merit, you have become this prince. Since the King of Karṇasuvarṇa (金耳國王) has destroyed the Buddha-dharma, you, in succeeding to the throne, should revive it; let compassion be your aim and sympathy dwell in your heart, and you will soon be the ruler of the five regions of India. If you wish to extend the prosperity of the state, you must follow my instructions; then, through hidden blessings, you will have no powerful enemies in the neighboring lands. Do not ascend the lion throne, and do not assume the title of Great King."  Thereupon, having received these instructions, he withdrew and assumed the throne, calling himself "The Prince" and taking the title Śīlāditya (尸羅阿迭多) (in the language of Tang, this means "Sun of Precepts"). He then said to his ministers, "The vengeance for my brother has not been requited, and the neighboring countries have not submitted; I shall not have a moment to eat with my right hand. Let all you officials be of one mind and exert your strength." He then gathered the national troops and trained his soldiers. He had 5,000 elephant troops, 20,000 cavalry, and 50,000 infantry, and from the west to the east, he campaigned against those who would not submit. Without the elephants being unsaddled or the men removing their armor, he brought the five regions of India into submission within six years. Having expanded his territory, he further increased his military forces, reaching 60,000 elephant troops and 100,000 cavalry. For nearly thirty years, the weapons of war were not raised, and the government and teachings were peaceful. He devoted himself to frugality, cultivated merit and goodness, and forgot both sleep and food. He ordered that no meat be eaten throughout the five regions of India, and if anyone took a life, they would be executed without pardon. Along the banks of the Ganges (gaṅgā), he erected several thousand stūpas, each over one hundred feet high. In the cities, villages, thoroughfares, and crossroads of the five regions of India, he established hospices (精廬) stocked with food, drink, and medicine to be distributed to travelers and the poor, providing for them without ceasing. At every site of a sacred relic, he built a monastery (saṅghārāma). Every five years, he held a great pan-charity assembly (pañcavārṣika), emptying the royal treasury to bestow gifts upon all beings, withholding only the weaponry from his charitable offerings. Every year, he gathered śramaṇas from various countries for a meeting lasting twenty-one days, during which he provided them with the four requisites, grandly decorated the Dharma seats and discussion halls, and had them engage in debate to assess their relative merits, praise the virtuous and criticize the evil, and demote the ignorant while promoting the enlightened. Those whose observance of the precepts was steadfast and whose moral character was profound were invited to ascend the lion seat, and the king would receive the Dharma from them in person. Those whose precepts were pure but whose learning was not grounded in the classics were merely treated with respect to show his veneration. Those who had no discipline and whose corrupt conduct was manifest were driven out of the country, as he did not wish to see or hear of them. If the minor rulers and assistant ministers of neighboring countries cultivated merit without ceasing and sought goodness without weariness, the king would take them by the hand to sit together and call them his "virtuous friends." If they were otherwise, he would not meet them face-to-face, and if there were matters to discuss, he would communicate only through the exchange of envoys. He toured the regions to inspect the customs of the people and did not have a fixed residence, building temporary huts wherever he stopped. Only during the three months of the rainy season did he cease traveling due to the heavy rains. At his temporary palaces, he would daily prepare fine meals to feed one thousand monks and five hundred Brahmins of various schools. He divided each day into three periods: one period for managing affairs and governing, and two periods for cultivating merit and practicing virtue. He was diligent and tireless, feeling that the day was never long enough. Initially, I had accepted an invitation from King Kumāra to travel from the country of Magadha (摩揭陀國) to the country of Kāmarūpa (迦摩縷波國). At that time, King Śīlāditya (戒日王) was on a tour of inspection in the country of Kajuṅghira (羯朱嗢祇羅國) and commanded King Kumāra, saying: "You should come quickly with the guest śramaṇa from Nālandā (那爛陀) to attend the assembly." Thereupon, I went with King Kumāra to meet him. After King Śīlāditya had offered greetings, he asked: "From what country have you come, and what is it that you seek?" I replied: "I have come from the Great Tang (大唐國) to seek the Buddha-Dharma." The king asked: "In what direction does the Great Tang lie? What is the extent of the route, and how far is it from here?" I replied: "It lies more than several tens of thousands of *li* to the northeast of here; it is what you in India call the country of Mahācīna (摩訶至那國)." The king said: "I have heard that in the country of Mahācīna there is a Son of Heaven, the Prince of Qin (秦王天子), who was perceptive and wise in his youth and has become divinely martial in his maturity. In the past, when the previous dynasty fell into chaos, the land was divided and collapsed, weapons of war arose on all sides, and the masses were poisoned by suffering. The Prince of Qin, however, early on cherished far-reaching strategies, aroused great compassion, rescued all sentient beings, and pacified the world. His civilizing influence reached far and wide, and his virtuous grace extended to distant places; strange lands and foreign regions admired his transformation and declared themselves his subjects. The people, having received his protection and nurturing, all sing the 'Music of the Prince of Qin Breaking the Ranks' (秦王破陣樂). I have heard these elegant hymns for a long time now. Is the reputation of his magnificent virtue truly as it is said? Is the Great Tang this country?" I replied, 'It is. Cīna (至那) was the name of the country under former kings; Great Tang is the title of my sovereign's realm. Before he ascended the throne, he was called the Prince of Qin; now that he has assumed the succession, he is titled the Son of Heaven. When the fortune of the previous dynasty ended, the masses were without a master, weapons of war arose in chaos, and living beings were cruelly harmed. The Prince of Qin, endowed by Heaven with vast magnanimity, felt compassion in his heart; his majestic influence stirred and spread, the various violent factions were exterminated, the eight directions were pacified, and ten thousand nations came to pay tribute. He loves and nurtures the four forms of birth, reveres and honors the Three Jewels, lightens taxes and levies, and reduces punishments; yet the state’s resources are abundant, and the common people have no need for hidden shelters. His civilizing influence and great transformation are difficult to fully describe.' King Śīlāditya (戒日王) said, 'Magnificent! The living beings of that land are blessed to be moved by such a holy lord.'  At that time, King Śīlāditya was about to return to the city of Kanyākubja (曲女城) to hold a religious assembly, followed by hundreds of thousands of people on the southern bank of the Ganges (殑伽河). King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) followed with tens of thousands of people, residing on the northern bank. They divided the river between them and advanced by both land and water. The two kings led the way, escorted by the four divisions of the army; some sailed in boats, others rode elephants, beating drums, blowing conches, and playing string and wind instruments. After ninety days, they reached the city of Kanyākubja, located in the Great Flower Wood to the west of the Ganges. At that time, more than twenty kings of various countries, having previously received the summons, arrived with the eminent śramaṇas, brahmans, officials, and soldiers of their respective kingdoms to gather for the great assembly. The King had previously built a large monastery (saṃghārāma) on the west side of the river. To the east of the monastery, he erected a precious terrace over one hundred feet high, in which was a golden Buddha image equal in size to the King’s own body. To the south of the terrace, he built a precious altar as a place to bathe the Buddha image. Fourteen or fifteen li to the northeast of this, he constructed a separate temporary palace. It was then the month of the middle of spring. From the first day of the month until the twenty-first, he provided delicious food to all the śramaṇas and brahmans. From the temporary palace to the monastery, pavilions were built along the sides of the road, decorated with every ornament, where musicians remained stationed, playing elegant music in succession.  The King brought out a golden image from the temporary palace, hollow and embossed, over three feet in height; it was loaded onto a large elephant and covered with a precious canopy. King Śīlāditya (戒日王), dressed in the attire of Indra (帝釋), held a precious canopy and attended on the left, while King Kumāra (拘摩羅王) assumed the guise of Brahmā (梵王), holding a white fly-whisk and attending on the right. Five hundred elephant-mounted soldiers on each side, clad in armor, provided a protective escort, while a hundred great elephants preceded and followed the Buddha image, carrying musicians who played music and beat drums. King Śīlāditya scattered pearls, various jewels, and gold and silver flowers at every step as an offering to the Three Jewels. First, they proceeded to the precious altar to bathe the image with perfumed water; then the King personally carried the image and escorted it to the western terrace, offering tens of hundreds of thousands of jewels and kauśeya garments as offerings. At that time, only twenty-some śramaṇas were permitted to follow, while the various kings served as guards. Once the meal was finished, he gathered the various heterodox scholars to discuss subtle doctrines and clarify profound principles. As the sun approached dusk, the King returned to his temporary palace. In this manner, he escorted the golden image daily, with the procession following as before, until the day of the dispersal. Suddenly, a fire broke out on the great terrace, and smoke and flames began to rage at the gatehouse of the monastery. The King said: "I have exhausted the treasures of the nation to build this monastery in honor of my late father, so as to manifest his magnificent achievements; yet my lack of virtue has left me without protection, resulting in such a disaster—with such an omen of calamity, what is the use of living!" He then burned incense, made a respectful petition, and took a vow, saying: "By the grace of my past good deeds, I have become a king over all India; may the power of my merit extinguish this fire, and if there is no spiritual response, I shall lose my life from this moment forth!" He immediately exerted himself, leaped across the threshold of the gate, and as if by some force extinguishing it, the fire died out and the smoke vanished. The various kings witnessed this miracle and their awe and reverence increased. Afterward, the King’s expression remained unchanged and his speech was as usual; he asked the various kings: "Suddenly this disaster has occurred, burning and destroying the finished work; what is in your hearts, and what are your thoughts?" The various kings prostrated themselves, weeping in sorrow, and replied: "This magnificent achievement was hoped to be passed on to future generations; now that it is reduced to ashes in an instant, how can we not be grieved? Furthermore, the various heterodox scholars are rejoicing in their hearts!" The King said: "Viewing it from this perspective, what the Tathāgata said is true. The heterodox scholars and those of different doctrines cling to the view of permanence, whereas only our Great Master teaches impermanence. However, my giving and renunciation have already been completed, and my heart’s desire has been fulfilled. Encountering this destruction, I have come to know once again the truthful teaching of the Tathāgata; this is a great good, and there is no reason for deep sorrow." Thereupon, he followed the various kings to the east to ascend the great stūpa to view the surroundings. Just as he was descending the steps, a strange man suddenly appeared holding a blade to confront the King. The King, in that moment of peril, retreated up the steps, bent down to seize the man, and handed him over to his officials. At that time, the officials were in a state of panic and did not know how to advance to rescue him. The various kings all requested that this man be executed, but King Śīlāditya (戒日王) showed no sign of anger and merely ordered that he not be killed. The King personally asked, "What have I done to wrong you that you would commit such a violent and evil act?" He replied, "Your Majesty’s virtuous grace is impartial, and both within and without the realm, all are indebted to you. However, I am mad and foolish; without considering the grander scheme, I was moved by a single word from the heretics to become an assassin and plot this treasonous murder." The King asked, "For what reason did the heretics harbor such evil intentions?" He replied, "Your Majesty has assembled the various nations and emptied the treasury to provide offerings to the śramaṇas and to cast Buddha images, yet the heretics, who were summoned from afar, have not been granted an audience; they truly feel ashamed and humiliated. This led me, in my madness and folly, to dare to commit this violent deception." Thereupon, the King investigated the followers of the heretics. There were five hundred Brahmins, all of them men of high talent, who had assembled by royal command; envious of the śramaṇas receiving the King's respect and honors, they shot fire-arrows to burn the precious terrace, hoping that in the ensuing chaos as people rushed to put out the fire, they could kill the Great King. Having found no other opportunity, they hired this man to rush into the narrow passage and carry out the assassination. At that time, the various kings and ministers requested that the heretics be executed, but the King only punished the ringleaders, left the remaining partisans unpunished, and banished the five hundred Brahmins from the borders of India. Thereupon, he returned to the capital.  To the northwest of the city is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here preaching various wonderful Dharmas. Beside it are the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.  To the south of the preaching stūpa, overlooking the Ganges (殑伽河) river, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having separate gates; the Buddha images are magnificent and beautiful, the monastic community is solemn and respectful, and they employ several thousand households of monastery servants (淨人). In the precious casket of the *vihāra* (精舍) is a tooth of the Buddha, over an inch and a half long, of extraordinary luster and changing colors, shifting from morning to evening. People from near and far flock there, and the gentry and commoners gather in great numbers, daily numbering a hundred thousand, to perform acts of veneration. Because the overseers were troubled by the noise and confusion, they provisionally established a heavy tax, announcing to those near and far: "Those who wish to see the Buddha's tooth must pay a large sum of gold." Nevertheless, the number of those coming to pay homage remained vast, and they were happy to compete in their hearts to pay the gold tax. On every fast day, it is brought out and placed on a high seat; hundreds of thousands of people burn incense and scatter flowers, and although the flowers pile up, the tooth casket is never submerged.  To the left and right in front of the monasteries, there is a *vihāra*, each over a hundred feet high, with stone foundations and brick chambers; the Buddha images within are adorned with various jewels, some cast in gold or silver, others smelted from brass (鍮石). In front of each of the two *vihāra*s is a small monastery. Not far to the southeast of the monastery, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) with stone foundations and brick chambers, over two hundred feet in height. Inside is a standing image of the Tathāgata, over thirty feet high, cast in brass (鍮石) and adorned with various wonderful jewels. On the stone walls surrounding the *vihāra*, the deeds experienced by the Tathāgata while practicing the bodhisattva path are carved and painted, fully and exhaustively engraved. Not far to the south of the stone *vihāra*, there is a temple to the Sun God (Āditya-deva). Not far to the south of that temple, there is a temple to Maheśvara (大自在天). Both are polished with blue stone and are equally exhaustive in their carvings; their scale and dimensions are the same as the Buddha’s *vihāra*. Each has a thousand households assigned to sweep and clean them, with drums, music, and singing continuing day and night without cessation. Six or seven li to the southeast of the great city, on the south bank of the Gaṅgā (殑伽河), there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). In the past, the Tathāgata spent six months here speaking on the impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity of the body. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There are also small stūpas containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata; when people are afflicted with illness, if they circumambulate them with utmost sincerity, they will certainly be cured and receive their blessings.

zh: 大城東南行百餘里，至納縛提婆矩羅城，據殑伽河東岸，周二十餘里。華林清池，互相影照。納縛提婆矩羅城西北，殑伽河東，有一天祠，重閣層臺，奇工異製。城東五里有三伽藍，同垣異門，僧徒五百餘人，並學小乘說一切有部。伽藍前二百餘步，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。基雖傾陷，尚高百餘尺，是如來昔於此處七日說法。中有舍利，時放光明。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。伽藍北三四里，臨殑伽河岸，有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。昔如來在此七日說法，時有五百餓鬼來至佛所，聞法解悟，捨鬼生天。說法窣堵波側有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。其側復有如來髮、爪窣堵波。
en_current: Traveling southeast from the great city for more than one hundred *li*, one arrives at the city of Navadevakula (納縛提婆矩羅城). It is situated on the eastern bank of the Ganges (殑伽河) and measures more than twenty *li* in circumference. Flowery groves and clear ponds reflect one another. To the northwest of the city of Navadevakula, on the east side of the Ganges, there is a temple to a deva, with multi-storied pavilions and terraced platforms, featuring extraordinary workmanship and unique construction. Five *li* to the east of the city, there are three monasteries (saṃghārāma) sharing the same wall but having different gates, with over five hundred monks who all study the Hīnayāna Sarvāstivāda school. Two hundred paces in front of the monasteries, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka. Although the base has collapsed and sunk, it is still over one hundred feet high; this is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for seven days. Inside it are relics that occasionally emit light. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Three or four *li* to the north of the monasteries, bordering the bank of the Ganges, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. Formerly, the Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for seven days, at which time five hundred hungry ghosts (preta) came to the Buddha’s presence, heard the Dharma, attained understanding, and, abandoning their ghost bodies, were reborn in heaven. Beside the stūpa of the preaching of the Dharma are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Beside that, there is also a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata.

zh: 自此東南行六百餘里，渡殑伽河，南至阿踰陀國（中印度境）。阿踰陀國，周五千餘里。國大都城周二十餘里。糓稼豐盛，華菓繁茂。氣序和暢，風俗善順，好營福，勤學藝。伽藍百有餘所，僧徒三千餘人，大乘、小乘，兼功習學。天祠十所，異道寡少。大城中有故伽藍，是伐蘇畔度菩薩（唐言世親。舊曰婆藪盤豆，譯曰天親。訛謬也）數十年中於此製作大小乘諸異論。其側故基，是世親菩薩為諸國王、四方俊彥、沙門、婆羅門等講義說法堂也。城北四五里，臨殑伽河岸，大伽藍中，有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。是如來為天、人眾，於此三月說諸妙法。其側窣堵波，過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。伽藍西四五里，有如來髮、爪窣堵波。髮、爪窣堵波北，伽藍餘趾，昔經部室利邏多（唐言勝受）論師於此製造經部《毘婆沙論》。城西南五六里大菴沒羅林中，有故伽藍，是阿僧伽（唐言無著）菩薩請益導凡之處。無著菩薩夜昇天宮，於慈氏菩薩所受《瑜伽師地論》、《莊嚴大乘經論》、《中邊分別論》等，晝為大眾講宣妙理。菴沒羅林西北百餘步，有如來髮、爪窣堵波。其側故基，是世親菩薩從覩史多天下見無著菩薩處。無著菩薩，健馱邏國人也，佛去世後一千年中，誕靈利見，承風悟道，從彌沙塞部出家修學，頃之迴信大乘。其弟世親菩薩於說一切有部出家受業，博聞強識，達學研機。無著弟子佛陀僧訶（唐言師子覺）者，密行莫測，高才有聞。二三賢哲每相謂曰：「凡修行業，願覲慈氏，若先捨壽，得遂宿心，當相報語，以知所至。」其後師子覺先捨壽命，三年不報。世親菩薩尋亦捨壽，時經六月，亦無報命。時諸異學咸皆譏誚，以為世親菩薩及師子覺，流轉惡趣，遂無靈鑒。其後無著菩薩於夜初分，方為門人教授定法，燈光忽翳，空中大明，有一天仙乘虛下降，即進階庭敬禮無著。無著曰：「爾來何暮？今名何謂？」對曰：「從此捨壽命，往覩史多天慈氏內眾蓮華中生，蓮華纔開，慈氏讚曰：『善來廣慧，善來廣慧。』旋繞纔周，即來報命。」無著菩薩曰：「師子覺者，今何所在？」曰：「我旋繞時，見師子覺在外眾中，耽著欲樂，無暇相顧，詎能來報？」無著菩薩曰：「斯事已矣。慈氏何相？演說何法？」曰：「慈氏相好，言莫能宣。演說妙法，義不異此。然菩薩妙音，清暢和雅，聞者忘倦，受者無厭。」無著講堂故基西北四十餘里，至故伽藍，北臨殑伽河，中有塼窣堵波，高百餘尺，世親菩薩初發大乘心處。世親菩薩自北印度至於此也，時無著菩薩命其門人，令往迎候。至此伽藍，遇而會見。無著弟子止戶牖外，夜分之後，誦《十地經》。世親聞已，感悟追悔：「甚深妙法，昔所未聞，誹謗之愆，源發於舌，舌為罪本，今宜除斷。」即執銛刀，欲自斷舌。乃見無著住立告曰：「夫大乘教者，至真之理也，諸佛所讚，眾聖攸宗。吾欲誨爾，爾今自悟。悟其時矣，何善如之？諸佛聖教，斷舌非悔。昔以舌毀大乘，今以舌讚大乘，補過自新，猶為善矣，杜口絕言，其利安在？」作是語已，忽不復見。世親承命，遂不斷舌。旦詣無著，諮受大乘。於是研精覃思，製大乘論，凡百餘部，並盛宣行。
en_current: From here, traveling southeast for more than six hundred li and crossing the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River, one arrives south at the country of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Ayodhyā is more than five thousand li in circuit. The capital city of the country is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are lush. The climate is temperate and pleasant, the customs are virtuous and compliant, and the people are fond of performing meritorious deeds and are diligent in studying the arts. There are more than one hundred monasteries and over three thousand monks, who study both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna teachings with equal effort. There are ten Deva temples, and there are few followers of heterodox paths. Within the great city is an old monastery; this is where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (伐蘇畔度) (in the language of Tang, *Shiqin* [世親]; formerly called *Posoupandou* [婆藪盤豆], translated as *Tianqin* [天親]; this is erroneous) spent several decades composing various treatises on the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. Beside it are the old foundations of the hall where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu lectured on the meaning of the teachings and expounded the Dharma for kings, talented scholars from the four quarters, śramaṇas, and brāhmaṇas. Four or five li to the north of the city, on the bank of the Gaṅgā River, within a large monastery, there is a stūpa over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. It was here that the Tathāgata preached the various wonderful teachings for three months to an assembly of gods and men. Beside it is a stūpa marking the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. Four or five li to the west of the monastery, there is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. To the north of the hair and nail stūpa are the remains of a monastery where the Sautrāntika master Śrīlabdha (translated into Chinese as Shengshou, "Victorious Reception") formerly composed the Sautrāntika *Vibhāṣā Śāstra*. In a large mango grove five or six li to the southwest of the city, there is an old monastery, which is the place where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga (translated into Chinese as Wuzhuo, "Unattached") sought instruction and guided the common people. At night, the Bodhisattva Asaṅga would ascend to the heavenly palace and receive the *Yogācārabhūmi Śāstra*, the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra Śāstra*, the *Madhyāntavibhāga Śāstra*, and others from the Bodhisattva Maitreya, while by day he would lecture and proclaim these profound principles to the great assembly. More than one hundred paces to the northwest of the mango grove, there is a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. The old foundation beside it is the place where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu descended from the Tuṣita Heaven to see the Bodhisattva Asaṅga.  The Bodhisattva Asaṅga was a man from the country of Gandhāra (健馱邏國). One thousand years after the Buddha passed away, he was born with spiritual insight and keen faculties; following the tradition, he awakened to the Way. He left the household life to study in the Mahīśāsaka school, but after a short time, he turned his faith to the Mahāyāna. His younger brother, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu, left the household life and received his training in the Sarvāstivāda school; he was widely learned and possessed a strong memory, having mastered the teachings and investigated their underlying mechanisms. Asaṅga’s disciple Buddhasimha (translated into Chinese as Shizijue, "Lion-Awakened") had a hidden practice that was unfathomable, and he was renowned for his high talent. These two or three sages would often say to one another: "In all our cultivation of practice, we vow to behold Maitreya. If one of us should pass away first, he must return to report and let the other know where he has gone." Afterward, Buddhasimha (Shizijue) passed away first, but for three years he sent no report. Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (Shiqin) also passed away shortly thereafter, and six months went by without any report. At that time, various heterodox practitioners all mocked them, believing that Bodhisattva Vasubandhu and Buddhasimha had been reborn in the evil realms and thus possessed no spiritual insight.  Later, in the first watch of the night, as Bodhisattva Asaṅga (Wuzhuo) was instructing his disciples in the methods of meditation, the lamp light suddenly dimmed and the air became brilliantly illuminated. A celestial being descended through the void, approached the courtyard, and paid homage to Asaṅga. Asaṅga asked, "Why have you come so late? What is your name now?"  He replied, "Upon departing this life, I was reborn in the inner assembly of Maitreya (Cishi) in the Tuṣita (Dushiduo) heaven, within a lotus flower. The moment the lotus opened, Maitreya praised me, saying, 'Welcome, Vast-Wisdom (Guanghui), welcome, Vast-Wisdom.' I had only just finished circling him once when I came to report."  Bodhisattva Asaṅga asked, "Where is Buddhasimha now?"  He replied, "When I was circling, I saw Buddhasimha in the outer assembly, indulging in sensual pleasures. He had no time to look at me, so how could he have come to report?"  Bodhisattva Asaṅga said, "That matter is finished. What is Maitreya’s appearance like, and what Dharma does he expound?"  He replied, "Maitreya’s physical marks and excellence are beyond the power of words to describe. The wonderful Dharma he expounds is not different in meaning from this [Dharma here], yet the Bodhisattva’s wonderful voice is clear, smooth, and harmonious; those who hear it forget their fatigue, and those who receive it are never satiated." More than forty li to the northwest of the old foundations of the lecture hall of Asaṅga (無著), one reaches an old monastery. It faces the Ganges (gaṅgā) River to the north and contains a brick stupa over a hundred feet high, marking the place where Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) first conceived the aspiration for the Mahayana. When Bodhisattva Vasubandhu arrived here from northern India, Bodhisattva Asaṅga ordered his disciples to go and welcome him. Upon arriving at this monastery, they met and gathered. A disciple of Asaṅga stopped outside the window and, after the middle of the night, recited the *Daśabhūmika-sūtra* (十地經). Having heard this, Vasubandhu became enlightened and filled with remorse, thinking, "This profound and wonderful Dharma is something I have never heard before. The fault of my slander originated from my tongue; since the tongue is the root of my offense, I should now cut it off." He immediately took up a sharp knife, intending to cut off his own tongue. Then he saw Asaṅga standing there, who told him, "The Mahayana teaching is the ultimate truth, praised by all Buddhas and revered by all sages. I wished to instruct you, and now you have realized it yourself. Since you have realized it at this time, what could be better? According to the holy teachings of the Buddhas, cutting off one's tongue is not repentance. In the past you used your tongue to revile the Mahayana, so now you should use your tongue to praise the Mahayana; to make amends and start anew is still a virtuous deed, but what benefit is there in remaining silent and speechless?" Having spoken these words, he suddenly disappeared. Vasubandhu followed the instruction and did not cut off his tongue. At dawn, he went to Asaṅga to consult him and receive the Mahayana. Thereupon, he refined his essence and pondered deeply, composing over a hundred Mahayana treatises, all of which were widely propagated and practiced.

zh: 從此東行三百餘里，渡殑伽河，北至阿耶穆佉國（中印度境）。阿耶穆佉國，周二千四五百里。國大都城臨殑伽河，周二十餘里。其氣序土宜，同阿踰陀國。人淳俗質，勤學好福。伽藍五所，僧徒千餘人，習學小乘正量部法。天祠十餘所，異道雜居。城東南不遠，臨殑伽河岸，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，高二百餘尺，是如來昔於此處三月說法。其側則有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。復有如來髮、爪青石窣堵波。其側伽藍，僧徒二百餘人，佛像莊飾，威嚴如在。臺閣宏麗，奇製欝起，是昔佛陀馱婆（唐言覺使）論師於此製說一切有部《大毘婆沙論》。
en_current: From here, traveling east for more than three hundred li and crossing the Ganges River (gaṅgā), one arrives north at the kingdom of Ayamukha (阿耶穆佉國) (within the borders of Central India). The kingdom of Ayamukha is two thousand four or five hundred li in circuit. The capital city of the kingdom borders the Ganges River and is more than twenty li in circuit. Its climate and soil conditions are the same as those of the kingdom of Ayodhyā (阿踰陀國). The people are honest and simple in their customs, diligent in study, and fond of meritorious deeds. There are five monasteries with over one thousand monks, who study the teachings of the Sāmmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than ten Deva temples, where followers of various sects live together. Not far to the southeast of the city, on the bank of the Ganges River, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high, which is the place where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for three months. Beside it are the sites of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa of blue stone containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. Beside it is a monastery with over two hundred monks; the Buddha images are adorned and majestic, as if he were still present. The towers and pavilions are magnificent, with unique structures rising high; this is where the master of treatises Buddhadāsa (佛陀馱婆) (in the language of the Tang, "Servant of the Buddha") formerly composed the *Abhidharma-mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* of the Sarvāstivāda school.

zh: 從此東南行七百餘里，渡殑伽河南、閻牟那河北，至鉢邏耶伽國（中印度境）。鉢邏耶伽國，周五千餘里。國大都城據兩河交，周二十餘里。稼穡滋盛，菓木扶疎。氣序和暢，風俗善順。好學藝，信外道。伽藍兩所，僧徒寡少，並皆習學小乘法教。天祠數百，異道寔多。大城西南瞻博迦華林中，有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也。基雖傾陷，尚百餘尺，在昔如來於此處降伏外道。其側則有髮、爪窣堵波、經行遺迹。髮、爪窣堵波側，有故伽藍，是提婆（唐言天受）菩薩作《廣百論》挫小乘、伏外道處。初，提婆菩薩自南印度至此伽藍，城中有外道婆羅門，高論有聞，辯才無礙，循名責實，反質窮辭。雅知提婆博究玄奧，欲挫其鋒，乃循名問曰：「汝為何名？」提婆曰：「名天。」外道曰：「天是誰？」提婆曰：「我。」外道曰：「我是誰？」提婆曰：「狗。」外道曰：「狗是誰？」提婆曰：「汝。」外道曰：「汝是誰？」提婆曰：「天。」外道曰：「天是誰？」提婆曰：「我。」外道曰：「我是誰？」提婆曰：「狗。」外道曰：「誰是狗？」提婆曰：「汝。」外道曰：「汝是誰？」提婆曰：「天。」如是循環，外道方悟。自時厥後，深敬風猷。
en_current: From here, traveling southeast for more than seven hundred li, crossing to the south of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) and the north of the Yamunā, one reaches the country of Prayāga (鉢邏耶伽國) (in the territory of Central India). The country of Prayāga is more than five thousand li in circuit. The great capital city of the country is situated at the confluence of the two rivers and is more than twenty li in circuit. The crops are abundant and lush, and the fruit trees are thick and spreading. The climate is harmonious and pleasant, and the customs are virtuous and compliant. The people are fond of learning the arts and believe in non-Buddhist paths. There are two monasteries with few monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna). There are several hundred deva temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous.  To the southwest of the great city, in a forest of Campaka (瞻博迦) flowers, there is a stūpa built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Although the base has collapsed and sunk, it is still more than one hundred feet high. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued non-Buddhists at this place. Beside it are the stūpas of the hair and nails, as well as traces of his walking meditation. Beside the hair and nail stūpas is an old monastery; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Deva (提婆) (in the language of the Tang, "Heaven-Received") composed the *Śataśāstra-vaipulya* (廣百論) to frustrate the Lesser Vehicle and subdue the non-Buddhists.  Formerly, when the Bodhisattva Deva came to this monastery from South India, there was a non-Buddhist Brahmin in the city who was renowned for his lofty arguments and possessed unimpeded eloquence; he would scrutinize names to demand their reality and use counter-interrogations to exhaust his opponents' words. Knowing that Deva was widely versed in profound mysteries and wishing to blunt his edge, he followed the name and asked, "What is your name?" Deva replied, "My name is Heaven (Deva)." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is Heaven?" Deva replied, "Me." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who am I?" Deva replied, "A dog." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven (Deva)." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is Heaven?" Deva replied, "Me." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who am I?" Deva replied, "A dog." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who is the dog?" Deva replied, "You." The non-Buddhist asked, "Who are you?" Deva replied, "Heaven." Through this cycle, the non-Buddhist finally attained realization. From that time forward, he deeply respected his noble conduct.

zh: 城中有天祠，瑩飾輪煥，靈異多端。依其典籍，此處是眾生殖福之勝地也，能於此祠捐捨一錢，功踰他所惠施千金。復能輕生，祠中斷命，受天福樂，悠永無窮。天祠堂前有一大樹，枝葉扶疎，陰影蒙密，有食人鬼依而棲宅，故其左右多有遺骸。若人至此祠中，無不輕捨身命，既怵邪說，又為神誘，自古迄今，習謬無替。近有婆羅門，族姓子也，闊達多智，明敏高才，來至祠中，謂眾人曰：「夫曲俗鄙志，難以導誘，吾方同事，然後攝化。」亦既登臨，俯謂友曰：「吾有死矣。昔謂詭妄，今驗真實，天仙伎樂依空接引，當從勝境捐此鄙形。」尋欲投身，自取殞絕，親友諫喻，其志不移。遂布衣服，遍周樹下，及其自投，得全軀命。久而醒曰：「唯見空中諸天召命，斯乃邪神所引，非得天樂也。」
en_current: In the city there is a temple to a deity, adorned and resplendent, with many varied manifestations of spiritual power. According to its scriptures, this place is a supreme site for sentient beings to cultivate merit; to donate a single coin at this temple yields merit exceeding a gift of a thousand gold pieces elsewhere. Furthermore, those who treat life lightly and end their existence within the temple receive heavenly bliss and joy, eternal and inexhaustible. In front of the temple hall stands a large tree with luxuriant branches and dense foliage, where a man-eating ghost (piśāca) has made its home; consequently, many skeletal remains lie scattered around it. When people come to this temple, they invariably throw away their lives, being both intimidated by perverse doctrines and enticed by the deity; from antiquity to the present, this erroneous practice has continued without change. Recently, there was a Brahmin, a son of a noble clan, who was magnanimous, wise, perceptive, and highly talented; he came to the temple and said to the crowd: "It is difficult to guide and transform those with crooked customs and base minds; I shall first join them in their actions and then lead them to conversion." Having ascended the tree, he looked down and said to his friends: "I am about to die. What I once considered a deception is now proven true; heavenly beings and celestial music are in the sky to receive me, and I shall abandon this base form to follow them to a superior realm." He immediately sought to cast himself down to end his life, and though his friends remonstrated with him, his resolve did not waver. He spread out his clothes all around beneath the tree, and when he threw himself down, he remained unharmed and his body was preserved. After a long while he regained consciousness and said: "I only saw various deities in the sky summoning me; this was the lure of evil spirits, not the attainment of heavenly bliss."

zh: 大城東，兩河交，廣十餘里，土地爽塏，細沙彌漫。自古至今，諸王、豪族，凡有捨施，莫不至止，周給不計，號大施場。今戒日王者，聿修前緒，篤述惠施，五年積財，一旦傾捨，於其施場，多聚珍貨。初第一日，置大佛像，眾寶莊嚴，即持上妙奇珍，而以奉施；次常住僧；次見前眾；次高才碩學、博物多能；次外道學徒，隱淪肥遁；次鰥寡孤獨，貧窮乞人。備極珍玩，窮諸上饌，如是節級，莫不周施。府庫既傾，服玩都盡，髻中明珠，身諸瓔珞，次第施與，初無所悔。既捨施已，稱曰：「樂哉！凡吾所有，已入金剛堅固藏矣。」從此之後，諸國君王各獻珍服。嘗不踰旬，府庫充仞。大施場東合流口，日數百人自溺而死。彼俗以為欲求生天，當於此處絕粒自沈，沐浴中流，罪垢消滅。是以異國遠方，相趁萃止，七日斷食，然後絕命。至於山猨、野鹿，群遊水濱，或濯流而返，或絕食而死。當戒日王之大施也，有一獼猴，居河之濱，獨在樹下屏迹絕食，經數日後自餓而死。故諸外道修苦行者，於河中立高柱，日將旦也，便即昇之，一手一足執柱端，躡傍杙，一手一足虛懸外申，臨空不屈，延頸張目，視日右轉，逮乎曛暮，方乃下焉。若此者，其徒數十，冀斯勤苦，出離生死，或數十年未嘗懈息。
en_current: To the east of the great city, where two rivers meet, the area is over ten *li* wide; the land is high and dry, covered with fine sand. From ancient times to the present, whenever kings and noble families have wished to perform acts of charity, they have all come to this place to distribute gifts without measure, and thus it is called the Grand Arena of Almsgiving (Mahādānapīṭha). The current King Śīlāditya (戒日王) continues the traditions of his predecessors and is devoted to the practice of charity; he accumulates wealth for five years and then, in a single day, empties his stores, gathering a vast quantity of precious goods at this arena. On the first day, a large statue of the Buddha is installed and adorned with various gems, and the most exquisite and rare treasures are offered to it. Next, offerings are made to the resident monks; then to the assembly present; then to those of high talent and profound learning, and those of broad knowledge and many skills; then to the disciples of non-Buddhist sects and those who live in seclusion; and finally to the widowed, the orphaned, the solitary, and the poor and destitute. Every kind of precious object is prepared and the finest foods are exhausted; in this graded order, everyone is provided for. Once the treasury is emptied and all clothing and ornaments are exhausted, he gives away the lustrous pearl in his topknot and the various necklaces on his body one after another, without the slightest regret. Having completed the distribution, he declares: "How joyful! All that I possessed has now been deposited into the indestructible treasury of the Vajra." Following this, the kings of various countries each offer him precious garments, and within ten days, his treasury is filled once again. At the confluence of the rivers to the east of the Grand Arena of Almsgiving, several hundred people drown themselves every day. The local custom holds that those who wish to be reborn in heaven should abstain from food and drown themselves at this spot, for by bathing in the middle of the current, their sins and defilements will be eradicated. For this reason, people from distant foreign lands flock here, fasting for seven days before ending their lives. As for the mountain apes and wild deer, they roam in groups along the riverbank; some return after washing in the current, while others fast until they die. During the great almsgiving of King Śīlāditya (戒日王), there was a macaque that lived by the riverbank, remaining alone under a tree, isolating itself and fasting, until it died of starvation after several days. Therefore, the various non-Buddhist ascetics (外道) who practice austerities plant tall pillars in the river. At the approach of dawn, they climb them, grasping the top of the pillar with one hand and one foot while stepping on a side peg, with the other hand and foot suspended and stretched out into the void, held straight without bending. They crane their necks and stare with wide eyes, watching the sun as it rotates to the right, and only when dusk falls do they descend. There are dozens of such followers who, hoping through this diligent suffering to escape the cycle of birth and death, have never slackened for several decades.

zh: 從此西南入大林中，惡獸、野象，群暴行旅，非多徒黨，難以經涉。行五百餘里，至憍賞彌國（舊曰拘睒彌國，訛也。中印度境）。憍賞彌國，周六千餘里。國大都城周三十餘里。土稱沃壤，地利豐植，粳稻多，甘蔗茂。氣序暑熱，風俗剛猛。好學典藝，崇樹福善。伽藍十餘所，傾頓荒蕪，僧徒三百餘人，學小乘教。天祠五十餘所，外道寔多。城內故宮中有大精舍，高六十餘尺，有刻檀佛像，上懸石蓋，鄔陀衍那王（唐言出愛。舊云優填王，訛也）之所作也。靈相間起，神光時照。諸國君王恃力欲舉，雖多人眾，莫能轉移。遂圖供養，俱言得真，語其源迹，即此像也。初，如來成正覺已，上昇天宮，為母說法，三月不還。其王思慕，願圖形像。乃請尊者沒特伽羅子，以神通力，接工人上天宮，親觀妙相，雕刻栴檀。如來自天宮還也，刻檀之像起迎世尊，世尊慰曰：「教化勞耶？開導末世，寔此為冀。」精舍東百餘步，有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。其側不遠，有如來井及浴室，井猶充汲，室以頹毀。
en_current: From here, traveling southwest into a great forest, one encounters ferocious beasts and wild elephants that attack travelers in herds; unless one has a large party, it is difficult to pass through. After traveling more than five hundred *li*, one arrives at the country of Kauśāmbī (憍賞彌國) (formerly called the country of Kausāmbi, which is incorrect; it is within the borders of Central India). The country of Kauśāmbī is over six thousand *li* in circumference. The capital city is over thirty *li* in circumference. The soil is described as fertile, the land is rich in produce, and there is much *śāli* rice and abundant sugarcane. The climate is hot, and the customs of the people are fierce and impetuous. They are fond of learning and the arts, and they esteem and cultivate merit and goodness. There are more than ten *saṃghārāmas*, which are dilapidated and overgrown, with over three hundred monks who study the teachings of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty *deva* temples, and the followers of non-Buddhist paths are very numerous. Within the old palace in the city, there is a large *vihāra* (精舍) over sixty feet high, housing a sandalwood Buddha image with a stone canopy suspended above it, which was made by King Udayana (鄔陀衍那王) (in the language of the Tang, "Giving Rise to Love"; formerly called King Youtian (優填王), which is erroneous). Miraculous signs appear from time to time, and divine light shines forth occasionally. Kings of various countries, relying on their strength, have wished to move it, but although they brought many people, none could shift it. Consequently, they have had copies made for worship, each claiming to have obtained the true likeness; when one speaks of their origin, it is indeed this very image. Initially, after the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he ascended to the heavenly palace to preach the Dharma for his mother, and for three months he did not return. The king, longing for him, wished to have his likeness made. He then requested the Venerable Maudgalyāyana to use his supernatural powers to transport an artisan to the heavenly palace to personally observe the Buddha's marvelous features and carve an image from sandalwood. When the Tathāgata returned from the heavenly palace, the sandalwood image rose to greet the World-Honored One, who consoled it, saying: "Have you been weary from the work of converting and guiding others? You are truly the hope for guiding those in the final age." More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery are the sites containing the traces of where the four past Buddhas sat and walked. Not far to the side are a well and a bathhouse used by the Tathāgata; the well still provides water for drawing, but the bathhouse has fallen into ruin.

zh: 城內東南隅，有故宅餘趾，是具史羅（舊云瞿師羅，訛也）長者故宅也，中有佛精舍及髮、爪窣堵波。復有故基，如來浴室也。城東南不遠，有故伽藍，具史羅長者舊園也。中有窣堵波，無憂王之所建立，高二百餘尺。如來於此數年說法。其側則有過去四佛座及經行遺迹之所，復有如來髮、爪窣堵波。伽藍東南重閣上有故塼室，世親菩薩嘗住此中作《唯識論》破斥小乘，難諸外道。伽藍東菴沒羅林中有故基，是無著菩薩於此作《顯揚聖教論》。城西南八九里，毒龍石窟。昔者如來伏此毒龍，於中留影，雖則傳記，今無所見。其側有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，高二百餘尺。傍有如來經行遺迹及髮、爪窣堵波，病苦之徒，求願多愈。釋迦法盡，此國最後，故上自君王，下及眾庶，入此國境，自然感傷，莫不飲泣，悲歎而歸。
en_current: In the southeast corner of the city are the remaining foundations of an old residence, which was the former home of the elder Ghoṣila (具史羅) (formerly called Qushiluo (瞿師羅), which is erroneous). Within it are a Buddha-*vihāra* (佛精舍) and a stupa containing hair and nail relics. There are also old foundations that were the bathhouse of the Tathāgata. Not far to the southeast of the city is an old monastery, which was the former garden of the elder Ghoṣila. Within it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. The Tathāgata preached the Dharma here for several years. Beside it are the seats of the four past Buddhas and the sites of their walking meditation, as well as another stupa containing the hair and nail relics of the Tathāgata. In a brick chamber on an upper story to the southeast of the monastery, the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu once resided and composed a treatise on consciousness-only (唯識論) to refute the Lesser Vehicle and challenge various non-Buddhist schools. In an Āmra (mango) grove to the east of the monastery are old foundations where the Bodhisattva Asaṅga composed the *Āryaśāsanaprakaraṇa* (顯揚聖教論). Eight or nine *li* to the southwest of the city is the stone cavern of a poisonous dragon. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued this poisonous dragon and left his shadow within it; although this is recorded in the chronicles, it cannot be seen today. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka, over two hundred feet high. Nearby are the sites of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation and a stupa containing his hair and nail relics; those suffering from illnesses who pray there are often healed. When the Dharma of Śākyamuni reaches its end, this country will be the last to remain; therefore, from the sovereign above down to the common people, all who enter the borders of this country naturally feel a sense of sorrow, and there is no one who does not weep and return home with sighs of lamentation.

zh: 龍窟東北大林中，行七百餘里，渡殑伽河，北至迦奢布羅城，周十餘里，居人富樂。城傍有故伽藍，唯餘基址，是昔護法菩薩伏外道處。此國先王扶於邪說，欲毀佛法，崇敬外道。外道眾中召一論師，聰敏高明達幽微者，作偽邪書千頌，凡三萬二千言，非毀佛法，扶正本宗。於是召集僧眾，令相摧論。外道有勝，當毀佛法；眾僧無負，斷舌以謝。是時僧徒懼有退負，集而議曰：「慧日已沈，法橋將毀，王黨外道，其可敵乎？事勢若斯，計將安出？」眾咸默然，無竪議者。護法菩薩年在幼稚，辯慧多聞，風範弘遠，在大眾中揚言贊曰：「愚雖不敏，請陳其略。誠宜以我疾應王命。高論得勝，斯靈祐也；徵議墮負，乃稚齒也。然則進退有辭，法、僧無咎。」僉曰：「允諧。」如其籌策。尋應王命，即昇論座。外道乃提頓綱網，抑揚辭義，誦其所執，待彼異論。護法菩薩納其言而笑曰：「吾得勝矣！將覆逆而誦耶？為亂辭而誦耶？」外道憮然而謂曰：「子無自高也。能領語盡，此則為勝，順受其文，後釋其義。」護法乃隨其聲調，述其文義，辭理不謬，氣韻無差。於是外道聞已，欲自斷舌。護法曰：「斷舌非謝，改執是悔。」即為說法，心信意悟。王捨邪道，遵崇正法。護法伏外道側，有窣堵波，無憂王所建也，基雖傾陷，尚高二百餘尺。是如來昔於此處六月說法。傍有經行之迹及髮、爪窣堵波。
en_current: Traveling over seven hundred li through a great forest to the northeast of the dragon cave and crossing the Ganges (gaṅgā) River, one arrives at the city of Kāśapura (迦奢布羅城), which is over ten li in circuit and whose inhabitants are wealthy and happy. Beside the city is an old monastery of which only the foundations remain; this is the place where the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla once subdued the heretics. A former king of this country supported heterodox views and wished to destroy the Buddha-dharma while venerating the heretics. From among the heretics, he summoned a master of treatises who was intelligent, brilliant, and well-versed in subtle mysteries to compose a fallacious and heterodox work of one thousand stanzas, totaling thirty-two thousand words, to slander the Buddha-dharma and establish his own sect as the orthodox one. Thereupon, he summoned the assembly of monks and ordered them to engage in a debate. If the heretics were victorious, the Buddha-dharma was to be destroyed; if the assembly of monks were not defeated, [the heretic] would cut out his tongue in atonement. At that time, the monks, fearing defeat, gathered and discussed the matter, saying, "The sun of wisdom has already set, and the bridge of the Dharma is about to be destroyed. The king sides with the heretics; how can we oppose them? With the situation as it is, what plan can we devise?" The assembly was silent, and no one could offer a suggestion. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla, though young in years, was eloquent, wise, and widely learned, with a character of great breadth. He spoke out in the midst of the assembly, saying, "Although I am not clever, I ask to present a brief proposal. It is truly appropriate that I should quickly respond to the king's command. If I win the high debate, it will be a spiritual blessing; if I am defeated in the inquiry, it will be attributed to my tender age. In this way, there will be an explanation whether I advance or retreat, and the Dharma and the Sangha will be without fault." Everyone said, "This is acceptable." He followed his plan, immediately responded to the king's command, and ascended the debate seat. The non-Buddhist (tīrthika) then laid out his main points, modulating his tone and meaning, and recited his own tenets, waiting for the opponent to raise objections. The Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法) accepted his words and laughed, saying, "I have already won! Shall I recite it in reverse order? Or shall I recite it with the words jumbled?" The non-Buddhist was taken aback and said to him, "Do not be arrogant. If you can repeat the words in their entirety, that will be victory; accept the text as it is, and then explain its meaning." Dharmapāla then followed his intonation and recited the text and its meaning; his phrasing and logic were not in error, and his tone and rhythm were without discrepancy. Upon hearing this, the non-Buddhist wanted to cut out his own tongue. Dharmapāla said, "Cutting the tongue is not an apology; changing one's views is repentance." He then preached the Dharma for him, and his heart became faithful and his mind enlightened. The king abandoned his heterodox path and followed and honored the true Dharma. Beside the place where Dharmapāla subdued the non-Buddhist, there is a stupa (窣堵波) built by King Aśoka (無憂王); although its foundation has subsided, it is still over two hundred feet high. This is where the Tathāgata formerly preached the Dharma for six months. Nearby are the traces of his walking meditation (caṅkrama) and a stupa containing his hair and nails.

zh: 伽藍東南重閣上有故塼室，世親菩薩嘗住此中作《唯識論》破斥小乘，難諸外道。
en_current: To the southeast of the monastery, on a multi-storied pavilion, there is an old brick chamber where the Bodhisattva Vasubandhu (世親) once resided to compose the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (唯識論), refuting the Hīnayāna and challenging various non-Buddhist philosophers.

zh: 城西南八九里，毒龍石窟。昔者如來伏此毒龍，於中留影，雖則傳記，今無所見。其側有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，高二百餘尺。傍有如來經行遺迹及髮、爪窣堵波，病苦之徒，求願多愈。
en_current: Eight or nine li to the southwest of the city is the stone cavern of the poisonous dragon. In the past, the Tathāgata subdued this poisonous dragon and left his shadow within it; although it is mentioned in the records, nothing can be seen there today. Beside it is a stūpa built by King Aśoka, which is over two hundred feet high. Nearby are the traces of the Tathāgata’s walking meditation, as well as a stūpa containing his hair and nail relics; those suffering from illnesses who pray there for recovery are mostly healed.

zh: 自此北行百七八十里，至鞞索（山格反）迦國（中印度境）。鞞索迦國，周四千餘里。國大都城周十六里。穀稼殷盛，華果具繁。氣序和暢，風俗淳質。好學不倦，求福不回。伽藍二十餘所，僧眾三千餘人，並學小乘正量部法。天祠五十餘所，外道甚多。城南道左，有大伽藍。昔提婆設摩阿羅漢於此造《識身論》，說無我人；瞿波阿羅漢作《聖教要實論》，說有我人。因此法執，遂深諍論。又是護法菩薩於此七日中摧伏小乘一百論師。伽藍側有窣堵波，高二百餘尺，無憂王所建也。如來昔日，六年於此說法導化。說法側有奇樹，高六七尺，春秋遞代，常無增減。是如來昔嘗淨齒，棄其遺枝，因植根柢，繁茂至今。諸邪見人及外道眾競來殘伐，尋生如故。其側不遠，有過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。復有如來髮、爪窣堵波。靈基連隅，林沼交映。從此東北行五百餘里，至室羅伐悉底國（舊曰舍衛，訛也。中印度境）。
en_current: Traveling northward from here for one hundred and seventy or eighty li, one arrives at the country of Viśākhā (鞞索迦國) (索 is read 山格反) (within the borders of Central India). The country of Viśākhā is over four thousand li in circuit. The capital city is sixteen li in circuit. The crops are abundant, and flowers and fruits are plentiful. The climate is temperate and pleasant, and the customs are honest and simple. The people are fond of learning without fatigue and are unswerving in their pursuit of merit. There are more than twenty saṃghārāmas and over three thousand monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Sāṃmitīya school of the Lesser Vehicle. There are more than fifty deva temples, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths. To the left of the road south of the city, there is a large saṃghārāma. In the past, the Arhat Devaśarman (提婆設摩) composed the *Vijñānakāya-śāstra* (識身論) here, which argues that there is no self or person; the Arhat Gopa (瞿波) composed the *Treatise on the Essential Truth of the Sacred Teaching* (聖教要實論), which argues that there is a self and a person. Because of this difference in doctrinal adherence, they engaged in deep debate. Furthermore, it was here that the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法) defeated one hundred masters of the Lesser Vehicle in seven days. Beside the saṃghārāma is a stūpa, over two hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka. In the past, the Tathāgata spent six years here preaching the Dharma and guiding the people. Beside the place where he preached is a marvelous tree, six or seven feet high; as spring and autumn succeed one another, it remains constant, neither increasing nor decreasing. It is said that the Tathāgata once cleaned his teeth here and discarded the twig, which then took root and has remained lush to this day. Various people of wrong views and followers of non-Buddhist paths have vied to cut it down, but it immediately grows back as it was before. Not far from there is the site of the seats and walking paths of the four past Buddhas. There is also a stūpa containing the hair and nails of the Tathāgata. The spiritual foundations are connected at the corners, and the woods and ponds reflect one another. Traveling northeast from here for more than five hundred li, one arrives at the country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) (formerly called Shewei, which is an error; it is within the borders of Central India).

zh: 室羅伐悉底國，周六千餘里。都城荒頓，疆埸無紀。宮城故基周二十餘里，雖多荒圮，尚有居人。穀稼豐，氣序和。風俗淳質，篤學好福。伽藍數百，圮壞良多，僧徒寡少，學正量部。天祠百所，外道甚多。此則如來在世之時，鉢邏犀那恃多王（唐言勝軍。舊曰波斯匿，訛略也）所治國都也。故宮城內有故基，勝軍王殿餘趾也。次東不遠，有一故基，上建小窣堵波，昔勝軍王為如來所建大法堂也。法堂側不遠，故基上有窣堵波，是佛姨母鉢邏闍鉢底（唐言生主。舊云波闍波提，訛也）苾芻尼精舍，勝軍王之所建立。次東窣堵波，是蘇達多（唐言善施。舊曰須達，訛也）故宅也。善施長者宅側有大窣堵波，是鴦窶利摩羅（唐言指鬘。舊曰央掘摩羅，訛也）捨邪之處，鴦窶利摩羅者，室羅伐悉底之凶人也。作害生靈，為暴城國，殺人取指，冠首為鬘。將欲害母，以充指數。世尊悲愍，方行導化。遙見世尊，竊自喜曰：「我今生天必矣。先師有教，遺言在茲，害佛殺母，當生梵天。」謂其母曰：「老今且止，先當害彼大沙門。」尋即杖劍往逆世尊。如來於是徐行而退，凶人指鬘疾驅不逮。世尊謂曰：「何守鄙志，捨善本，激惡源？」時指鬘聞誨，悟所行非，因即歸命，求入法中，精勤不怠，證羅漢果。
en_current: The country of Śrāvastī (室羅伐悉底國) is over 6,000 li in circuit. The capital city is desolate and ruined, and its boundaries are not clearly defined. The old foundations of the palace city are over 20 li in circuit; although it is largely ruined and overgrown, there are still inhabitants. The grain crops are abundant, and the climate is temperate. The customs are honest and simple, and the people are devoted to learning and fond of merit. There are several hundred monasteries, most of which are in ruins, and the number of monks is small; they study the Sammatiya (正量部) school. There are one hundred deva temples, and there are many followers of non-Buddhist paths.  This was the capital city governed by King Prasenajit (鉢邏犀那恃多王; in Chinese, Shengjun [Victorious Army]; the old term, Bosini (波斯匿), is a corruption and abbreviation) during the time the Tathāgata was in the world. Within the old palace city, there are old foundations, which are the remaining traces of the palace of King Prasenajit. Not far to the east, there is an old foundation upon which a small stupa is built; this was the Great Dharma Hall that King Prasenajit formerly built for the Tathāgata. Not far from the side of the Dharma Hall, there is a stupa on old foundations; this is the nunnery of the Buddha’s maternal aunt, Prajāpatī (鉢邏闍鉢底; in Chinese, Shengzhu [Lord of Life]; the old term, Bozhebotí (波闍波提), is a corruption), which was built by King Prasenajit. To the east of this is a stupa, which is the former residence of Sudatta (蘇達多; in Chinese, Shanshi [Well-Bestowing]; the old term, Xuda, is a corruption). Beside the residence of the elder Sudatta, there is a large stupa; this is the place where Aṅgulimāla (鴦窶利摩羅; in Chinese, Zhiman [Finger-Garland]; the old term, Yangjuemoluo (央掘摩羅), is a corruption) abandoned his evil ways. Aṅgulimāla was a violent man of Śrāvastī. He harmed living beings and committed atrocities in the city and the country, killing people to take their fingers and wearing them on his head as a garland. He was about to kill his mother to complete the count of his fingers. The World-honored One, moved by compassion, set out to guide and transform him. Seeing the World-honored One from afar, he secretly rejoiced and said, "I am now certain to be reborn in heaven. My former teacher gave me instructions, and his legacy is here: by killing a Buddha and killing one's mother, one shall be reborn in the Brahmā heaven." He said to his mother, "Old lady, stay here for now; I must first kill that great śramaṇa." He immediately took up his sword and went to intercept the World-honored One. The Tathāgata then retreated at a slow pace, yet the wicked Aṅgulimāla could not catch up even though he ran fast. The World-honored One said to him, "Why do you persist in your base intentions, abandoning the root of goodness and stirring up the source of evil?" At that time, Aṅgulimāla heard this instruction and realized that his actions were wrong; he then took refuge, sought to enter the Dharma, practiced diligently without slackening, and attained the fruit of an Arhat.

zh: 城南五六里，有逝多林（唐言勝林。舊曰祇陀，訛也），是給孤獨園。勝軍王大臣善施為佛建精舍，昔為伽藍，今已荒廢。東門左右各建石柱，高七十餘尺，左柱鏤輪相於其端，右柱刻牛形於其上，並無憂王之所建也。室宇傾圮，唯餘故基，獨一甎室巋然獨在，中有佛像。昔者如來昇三十三天，為母說法之後，勝軍王聞出愛王刻檀像佛，乃造此像。善施長者仁而聰敏，積而能散，拯乏濟貧，哀孤恤老，時美其德，號給孤獨焉。聞佛功德，深生尊敬，願建精舍，請佛降臨。世尊命舍利子隨瞻揆焉，唯太子逝多園地爽塏。尋詣太子，具以情告。太子戲言：「金遍乃賣。」善施聞之，心豁如也，即出藏金，隨言布地。有少未滿，太子請留，曰：「佛誠良田，宜植善種。」即於空地，建立精舍。世尊即之，告阿難曰：「園地善施所買，林樹逝多所施，二人同心，式崇功業。自今已去，應謂此地為逝多林給孤獨園。」給孤獨園東北有窣堵波，是如來洗病苾芻處。昔如來之在世也，有病苾芻，含苦獨處。世尊見而問曰：「汝何所苦？汝何獨居？」曰：「我性疎嬾，不耐看病，故今嬰疾，無人瞻視。」如來是時愍而告曰：「善男子，我今看汝。」以手拊摩，病苦皆愈。扶出戶外，更易敷蓐，親為盥洗，改著新衣。佛語苾芻：「當自勤勵。」聞誨感恩，心悅身豫。給孤獨園西北有小窣堵波，是沒特伽羅子運神通力舉舍利子衣帶不動之處。昔佛在無熱惱池，人、天咸集，唯舍利子不時從會。佛命沒特伽羅往召來集。沒特伽羅承命而往，舍利子補護法衣。沒特伽羅曰：「世尊今在無熱惱池，命我召爾。」舍利子曰：「且止，須我補竟，與子偕行。」沒特伽羅曰：「若不速行，欲運神力，舉爾石室至大會所。」舍利子乃解衣帶置地，曰：「若舉此帶，我身或動。」時沒特伽羅運大神通，舉帶不動，地為之震。因以神足還詣佛所，見舍利子已在會坐。沒特伽羅俛而歎曰：「乃今以知，神通之力不如智慧之力矣。」舉帶窣堵波側不遠，有井。如來在世，汲充佛用。其側有窣堵波，無憂王之所建也，中有如來舍利。經行之迹，說法之處，並樹旌表，建窣堵波。冥祇警衛，靈瑞間起，或鼓天樂，或聞神香，景福之祥，難以備敘。伽藍後不遠，是外道梵志殺婬女以謗佛處。如來十力無畏，一切種智，人、天宗仰，聖賢遵奉。時諸外道共相議曰：「宜行詭詐，眾中謗辱。」乃誘雇婬女，詐為聽法，眾所知已，密而殺之，埋屍樹側，稱怨告王。王命求訪，於逝多園得其屍焉。是時外道高聲唱言：「喬答摩大沙門常稱戒忍，今私此女，殺而滅口。既婬既殺，何戒何忍？」諸天空中隨聲唱曰：「外道凶人為此謗耳。」伽藍東百餘步，有大深坑，是提婆達多欲以毒藥害佛，生身陷入地獄處。提婆達多（唐言天授），斛飯王之子也。精勤十二年，已誦持八萬法藏。後為利故，求學神通，親近惡友，共相議曰：「我相三十，減佛未幾；大眾圍繞，何異如來？」思惟是已，即事破僧。舍利子、沒特伽羅子奉佛指告，承佛威神，說法誨喻，僧復和合。提婆達多惡心不捨，以惡毒藥置指爪中，欲因作禮，以傷害佛。方行此謀，自遠而來，至於此也，地遂坼焉，生陷地獄。其南復有大坑，瞿伽梨苾芻毀謗如來，生身陷入地獄。瞿伽梨陷坑南八百餘步，有大深坑，是戰遮婆羅門女毀謗如來，生身陷入地獄之處。佛為人、天說諸法要，有外道弟子，遙見世尊大眾恭敬，便自念曰：「要於今日辱喬答摩，敗其善譽，當令我師獨擅芳聲。」乃懷繫木盂，至給孤獨園，於大眾中揚聲唱曰：「此說法人與我私通，腹中之子乃釋種也。」邪見者莫不信然，貞固者知為訕謗。時天帝釋欲除疑故，化為白鼠，齧斷盂系，系斷之聲震動大眾，凡諸見聞增深喜悅。眾中一人起持木盂，示彼女曰：「是汝兒耶？」是時也，地自開坼，全身墜陷，入無間獄，具受其殃。凡此三坑，洞無涯底，秋夏霖雨，溝池泛溢，而此深坑，嘗無水止。伽藍東六七十步，有一精舍，高六十餘尺，中有佛像，東面而坐。如來在昔，於此與諸外道論議。次東有天祠，量等精舍。日旦流光，天祠之影不蔽精舍；日將落照，精舍之陰遂覆天祠。影覆精舍東三四里，有窣堵波，是尊者舍利子與外道論議處。初，善施長者買逝多太子園，欲為如來建立精舍。時尊者舍利子隨長者而瞻揆，外道六師求角神力，舍利子隨事攝化，應物降伏。其側精舍前建窣堵波，如來於此摧諸外道，又受毘舍佉母請。受請窣堵波南，是毘盧釋迦王（舊曰毘琉離主，訛也）興甲兵誅釋種，至此見佛歸兵之處。毘盧釋迦王嗣位之後，追怨前辱，興甲兵，動大眾，部署已畢，申命方行。時有苾芻聞以白佛，世尊於是坐枯樹下。毘盧釋迦王遙見世尊，下乘禮敬，退立言曰：「茂樹扶疎，何故不坐？枯株朽櫱，而乃遊止？」世尊告曰：「宗族者，枝葉也。枝葉將危，庇蔭何在？」王曰：「世尊為宗親耳，可以迴駕。」於是覩聖感懷，還軍返國。還軍之側，有窣堵波，是釋女被戮處。毘盧釋迦王誅釋克勝，簡五百女，充實宮闈。釋女憤恚，怨言不遜，詈其王：「家人之子也。」王聞發怒，命令誅戮。執法者奉王教，刖其手足，投諸阬阱。時諸釋女含苦稱佛，世尊聖鑒，照其苦毒，告命苾芻，攝衣而往，為諸釋女說微妙法，所謂羈纏五欲，流轉三途，恩愛別離，生死長遠。時諸釋女聞佛指誨，遠塵離垢，得法眼淨，同時命終，俱生天上。時天帝釋化作婆羅門，收骸火葬，後人記焉。誅釋窣堵波側不遠，有大涸池，是毘盧釋迦王陷身入地獄處。世尊觀釋女已，還給孤獨園，告諸苾芻，今毘盧釋迦王却後七日，為火所燒。王聞佛記，甚懷惶懼。至第七日，安樂無危。王用歡慶，命諸宮女往至河側，娛遊樂飲。猶懼火起，鼓棹清流，隨波泛濫。熾焰飈發，焚輕舟，墜王身，入無間獄，備受諸苦。
en_current: Five or six *li* south of the city is the Jetavana (逝多林; in the language of the Tang, "Victory Grove"; the old term "Qituo" (祇陀) is a corruption), which is the Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma (給孤獨園). The minister Sudatta (善施) of King Prasenajit (勝軍王) built a vihāra (精舍) for the Buddha; it was formerly a monastery, but now it lies in ruins. To the left and right of the east gate stand stone pillars over seventy feet high; the left pillar is topped with a carved wheel, and the right pillar is surmounted by the figure of a bull, both of which were erected by King Aśoka (無憂王). The buildings have collapsed, leaving only the old foundations, save for a single brick chamber that stands alone and intact, containing an image of the Buddha. Formerly, after the Tathāgata had ascended to the Trāyastriṃśa heaven to preach the Dharma for his mother, King Prasenajit heard that King Udayana (出愛王) had carved a sandalwood image of the Buddha, and he thereupon had this image made. The Elder Sudatta was benevolent and intelligent; he accumulated wealth only to distribute it, rescuing the needy, relieving the poor, and showing compassion to the orphaned and the aged. People of the time praised his virtues and called him Anāthapiṇḍada ("the Giver to the Orphaned and Solitary"). Having heard of the Buddha’s merits, he developed a deep sense of reverence and wished to build a vihāra and invite the Buddha to descend. The World-Honored One commanded Śāriputra to accompany him to survey the land, and they found that only the garden of Prince Jeta (逝多太子) was high and dry. He immediately went to the Prince and explained his intentions in full. The Prince jokingly said, "If you cover the ground with gold, I will sell it." Upon hearing this, Sudatta’s heart was filled with joy; he immediately brought out his hidden gold and covered the ground as he had said. There was a small portion left uncovered, and the Prince requested to keep it, saying, "The Buddha is truly a fertile field; it is fitting to plant good seeds there." He then built the vihāra on the vacant land. The World-Honored One went there and said to Ānanda, "The garden ground was purchased by Sudatta (善施), and the trees were donated by Jeta (逝多); the two men were of one mind, and thus they jointly established this meritorious work. From now on, this place shall be called the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma (逝多林給孤獨園)."  To the northeast of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a stūpa, which is the place where the Tathāgata washed a sick bhikṣu. Formerly, when the Tathāgata was in the world, there was a sick bhikṣu who was suffering and living alone. The World-Honored One saw him and asked, "What is your suffering? Why do you live alone?" He replied, "I am by nature lazy and cannot endure nursing the sick; therefore, I am now afflicted with illness, and there is no one to look after me." At that time, the Tathāgata felt compassion and said to him, "Good man, I will now nurse you." He stroked him with his hand, and his illness and suffering were all healed. He helped him out of the room, changed his bedding, personally washed him, and put new clothes on him. The Buddha said to the bhikṣu, "You should be diligent and exert yourself." Hearing this instruction, he felt gratitude, and his heart was joyful and his body at ease.  To the northwest of the Jetavana-anāthapiṇḍikārāma is a small stūpa, which is the place where Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) exercised his supernatural power to lift Śāriputra’s (舍利子) robe and belt, but could not move them. Formerly, when the Buddha was at Lake Anavatapta (無熱惱池), humans and devas had all gathered, but only Śāriputra did not arrive at the assembly in time. The Buddha ordered Maudgalyāyana to go and summon him to join the gathering. Maudgalyāyana accepted the command and went; Śāriputra was mending his dharma-robe. Maudgalyāyana said, "The World-Honored One is now at Lake Anavatapta and has ordered me to summon you." Śāriputra (舍利子) said, "Wait a moment; I must finish mending this, and then I will go with you." Maudgalyāyana (沒特伽羅) said, "If you do not go quickly, I shall use my supernatural power to lift your stone chamber and take it to the great assembly." Śāriputra then untied his robe and belt, placed them on the ground, and said, "If you can lift this belt, my body might move." At that time, Maudgalyāyana exerted his great supernatural power, but he could not lift the belt, and the earth shook because of it. He then used his supernatural foot-power to return to the place of the Buddha, where he saw that Śāriputra was already seated in the assembly. Maudgalyāyana bowed his head and sighed, saying, "Only now do I know that the power of supernatural abilities is not equal to the power of wisdom."  Not far from the stupa of the belt, there is a well. When the Tathāgata (如來) was in the world, water was drawn from it for the Buddha’s use. Beside it is a stupa built by King Aśoka (無憂王), which contains relics of the Tathāgata. The sites of his walking meditation and the places where he preached the Dharma are all marked with signs and have stupas built upon them. Dark spirits guard and protect them, and miraculous signs appear from time to time; sometimes heavenly music is played, and sometimes divine incense is smelled. The auspicious omens of these blessings are difficult to describe in full.  Not far behind the monastery is the place where the non-Buddhist ascetics (外道梵志) murdered a courtesan to slander the Buddha. The Tathāgata possesses the ten powers, the fearlessnesses, and the omniscience of all modes; he is revered by humans and devas, and honored by sages and worthies. At that time, the various non-Buddhists consulted together, saying, "We should employ deceit and slander him in the midst of the assembly." They then enticed and hired a courtesan, pretending she was coming to listen to the Dharma, and once this was known to the assembly, they secretly murdered her, buried her corpse beside a tree, and complained to the king, claiming injury. The king ordered a search, and her body was found in the Jetavana (逝多園). At that time, the non-Buddhists loudly proclaimed: "The great śramaṇa Gautama (喬答摩) always praises precepts and patience; now he has had illicit relations with this woman and killed her to silence her. Having committed both lechery and murder, where are his precepts and where is his patience?" The devas in the sky responded in unison, saying: "The wicked non-Buddhists have fabricated this slander."  More than one hundred paces to the east of the monastery is a large, deep pit; this is the place where Devadatta (提婆達多), intending to harm the Buddha with poison, fell alive into hell. Devadatta (in Chinese, "Heaven-bestowed") was the son of King Droṇodana (斛飯王). He practiced diligently for twelve years and had already memorized the eighty thousand sections of the Dharma-store. Later, for the sake of profit, he sought to learn supernatural powers and associated with evil friends, consulting with them: "My physical marks are thirty; they are not much less than the Buddha's.
