The Arhat said, "Your Majesty should command the spirits and deities that on the appointed day, when the sun is obscured by a shape like a hand, that is the moment to enshrine the relics." The King accepted this instruction and proclaimed it to the spirits and deities. When the appointed day arrived, King Aśoka observed the sunlight; at high noon, the Arhat used his supernatural power to stretch out his hand and block the sun, which was witnessed by all at the construction sites, and at this very moment, the works were all completed.  Not far from the side of the stūpa, there is a large stone within a *vihāra* (精舍) where the Tathāgata once stepped, and his twin footprints still remain; they are one foot eight inches long and over six inches wide. Both footprints possess the mark of a wheel, all ten toes are adorned with floral patterns, and the shape of a fish is clearly visible, emitting light from time to time. In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to attain extinction, he proceeded north toward the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸那城) and looked back south at the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國); standing upon this stone, he told Ānanda, "I now leave these last footprints here as I am about to enter extinction, looking back at Magadha. One hundred years after my passing, there will be a King Aśoka who will rule the world, establish his capital in this land, protect the Three Jewels, and command the hundred spirits." When King Aśoka (無憂王) succeeded to the throne, he moved the capital and built a city, enclosing the stone with the footprints (迹石) within it. As it was near the palace city, he constantly made offerings to it in person. Later, various kings competed to carry it away, but although the stone was not large, no one could move it. Recently, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) destroyed the Buddha-dharma and went to the site of the stone, intending to obliterate the holy relic; however, after he chiseled it, the surface became smooth again and the patterns remained as before, so he threw it into the Ganges River (殑伽河), but it soon returned to its original place. The stupa (窣堵波) beside it is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.

zh: 佛迹精舍側不遠，有大石柱，高三十餘尺，書記殘缺，其大略曰：「無憂王信根貞固，三以贍部洲施佛、法、僧，三以諸珍寶重自酬贖。」其辭云，大略斯在。故宮北有大石室，外若崇山，內廣數丈，是無憂王為出家弟役使神鬼之所建也。初，無憂王有同母弟，名摩醯因陀羅（唐言大帝）。生自貴族，服僣王制，奢侈縱暴，眾庶懷怨。國輔老臣進諫王曰：「驕弟作威，亦已太甚。夫政平則國治，人和則主安，古之則訓，由來久矣。願存國典，收付執法。」無憂王泣謂弟曰：「吾承基緒，覆燾生靈，況爾同胞，豈忘惠愛！不先匡導，已陷刑法。上懼先靈，下迫眾議。」摩醯因陀羅稽首謝曰：「不自謹行，敢干國憲，願賜再生，更寬七日。」於是置諸幽室，嚴加守衛，珍羞上饌，進奉無虧。守者唱曰：「已過一日，餘有六日。」至第六日已，既深憂懼，更勵身心，便獲果證，昇虛空，示神迹，尋出塵俗，遠棲巖谷。無憂王躬往謂曰：「昔拘國制，欲致嚴刑。豈意清昇，取證聖果。既無滯累，可以還國。」弟曰：「昔羈愛網，心馳聲色，今出危城，志悅山谷。願棄人間，長從丘壑。」王曰：「欲靜心慮，豈必幽巖？吾從爾志，當為崇樹。」遂召命鬼神而告之曰：「吾於後日廣備珍羞，爾曹相率來集我會，各持大石，自為床座。」諸神受命，至期畢萃。眾會既已，王告神曰：「石座從橫，宜自積聚。因功不勞，壘為虛室。」諸神受命，不日而成。無憂王躬往迎請，止此山廬。故宮北，地獄南，有大石槽，是無憂王匠役神功，作為此器，飯僧之時，以儲食也。故宮西南有小石山，周巖谷間，數十石室，無憂王為近護等諸阿羅漢，役使鬼神之所建立。傍有故臺，餘基積石；池沼漣漪，清瀾澄鑒，隣國遠人謂之聖水，若有飲濯，罪垢消滅。山西南有五窣堵波，崇基已陷，餘址尚高，遠而望之，欝若山阜，面各數百步，後人於上重更修建小窣堵波。《印度記》曰：「昔無憂王建八萬四千窣堵波已，尚餘五斗舍利，故別崇建五窣堵波，制奇諸處，靈異間起，以表如來五分法身。薄信之徒竊相評議，云是昔者難陀王建此藏，以儲七寶。其後有王，不甚淳信，聞先疑議，肆其貪求，興動軍師，躬臨發掘，地震山傾，雲昏日翳，窣堵波中大聲雷震，士卒僵仆，象馬驚奔。自茲已降，無敢覬覦。」或曰：「眾議雖多，未為確論；循古所記，信得其實。」
en_current: Not far from the side of the Vihara of the Buddha’s Footprints, there is a large stone pillar over thirty feet high. The inscription is incomplete, but its general meaning is: "King Aśoka’s (無憂王) roots of faith were firm and solid; he thrice offered Jambudvīpa to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and thrice redeemed it with various precious treasures." This is the general gist of the text.  To the north of the old palace is a large rock chamber; from the outside it appears like a high mountain, and inside it is several zhang wide. It was built by King Aśoka for his younger brother who had left home to become a monk, by employing spirits and ghosts.  Originally, King Aśoka had a younger brother by the same mother named Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅; in the language of Tang, "Great Emperor"). Born into the nobility, he wore clothing that usurped royal regulations and was extravagant, indulgent, and violent, causing the masses to harbor resentment. An old minister who assisted the state remonstrated with the King, saying, "Your arrogant brother’s exercise of power has already become too excessive. When government is equitable, the state is well-ordered; when the people are harmonious, the ruler is secure. This is an ancient maxim that has existed for a long time. I hope you will uphold the state laws and hand him over to the authorities."  King Aśoka wept and said to his brother, "I have inherited the foundation of the ancestors and provide shelter to all living beings; how could I forget the affection for you, my own flesh and blood? Yet, because I did not guide you earlier, you have already fallen into the trap of criminal law. Above, I fear the ancestral spirits; below, I am pressured by the public consensus."  Mahendra bowed his head and apologized, saying, "I did not conduct myself with prudence and dared to violate the national constitution. I pray you grant me a new lease on life by allowing a seven-day respite." Thereupon, he was placed in a secluded chamber, strictly guarded, and provided with fine delicacies and superior food, served without fail. The guard called out, "One day has passed; six days remain." When the sixth day had ended, having felt deep anxiety and fear, he further exerted his body and mind, whereupon he attained the fruit of enlightenment, ascended into the void, and manifested divine miracles; soon after, he left the secular world to dwell far away in a rocky valley. King Aśoka (無憂王) went in person and said to him, "Formerly, I was bound by state law and intended to impose a severe punishment. Who would have thought you would transcend so purely and attain the holy fruit? Since you are no longer burdened by attachments, you may return to the country." The younger brother replied, "Formerly, I was fettered by the net of desire, my mind racing after sights and sounds; now that I have escaped the city of danger, my will finds joy in the mountain valleys. I wish to abandon the human world and dwell forever among the hills and ravines." The king said, "To quiet the mind and thoughts, must one necessarily seek a secluded cliff? I shall follow your will and build a retreat for you." He then summoned the spirits and deities and told them, "On a coming day I shall prepare a grand feast of delicacies; you shall lead one another to gather at my assembly, each bringing a large stone to serve as your own seat." The spirits received the command and gathered in full by the appointed time. When the assembly had ended, the king said to the spirits, "The stone seats are scattered about; you should stack them up yourselves. Without laboring over the work, pile them into a chamber." The spirits received the command and completed it in a few days. King Aśoka went in person to invite him to stay in this mountain hut. North of the old palace and south of the hell, there is a large stone trough; it was through the divine labor of King Aśoka’s craftsmen that this vessel was created to store food when providing meals for the monks. To the southwest of the old palace is a small rocky mountain. Within its surrounding cliffs and valleys are several dozen stone chambers, which King Aśoka (無憂王) had built by employing spirits for the sake of the arhat Upagupta (近護) and others. Beside them is an old terrace with stone foundations remaining. There is a pond with rippling water, clear and limpid like a mirror; people from neighboring countries and distant lands call it the "holy water," and if one drinks from it or washes in it, one’s sins and defilements are eradicated.  To the southwest of the mountain are five stupas. Their lofty foundations have subsided, yet the remaining sites are still high; viewed from afar, they appear like lush mounds, each side measuring several hundred paces. People of later generations have built small stupas atop them. The *Record of India* (印度記) states: "In the past, after King Aśoka had built eighty-four thousand stupas, there remained five *dou* of relics; therefore, he specially constructed these five stupas, with a design surpassing all other places, where miracles occur from time to time to represent the fivefold Dharma-body (五分法身) of the Tathāgata." Those of shallow faith have secretly speculated that this was a treasury built by the former King Nanda (難陀王) to store the seven treasures. Later, there was a king who was not very sincere in his faith; hearing these earlier speculations, he gave free rein to his greed and desire. He mobilized his army and generals and came in person to excavate them. The earth shook and the mountains tilted, clouds darkened and the sun was obscured, and a great sound like thunder shook from within the stupas. The soldiers fell down stiff, and the elephants and horses fled in terror. Ever since then, no one has dared to covet them. Some say: "Although there are many public opinions, they are not definitive conclusions; by following the ancient records, one can obtain the truth."

zh: 王故宮北有石柱，高數十尺，是無憂王作地獄處。釋迦如來涅槃之後第一百年，有阿輸迦（唐言無憂。舊曰阿育，訛也）王者，頻毘婆羅（唐言影堅。舊曰頻婆娑，訛也）王之曾孫也，自王舍城遷都波吒釐，築外郭，周於故城。年代浸遠，唯餘故基。伽藍、天祠及窣堵波，餘址數百，存者二三。唯故宮北，臨殑伽河，小城中有千餘家。初，無憂王嗣位之後，舉措苛暴，乃立地獄，作害生靈。周垣峻峙，隅樓特起，猛焰洪鑪，銛鋒利刃，備諸苦具，擬像幽塗，招募凶人，立為獄主。初以國中犯法罪人，無挍輕重，總入塗炭。後以行經獄次，擒以誅戮，至者皆死，遂滅口焉。時有沙門，初入法眾，巡里乞食，遇至獄門，獄吏凶人擒欲殘害。沙門惶怖，請得禮懺。俄見一人，縛來入獄，斬截手足，磔裂形骸，俯仰之間，支體糜散。沙門見已，深增悲悼，成無常觀，證無學果。獄卒曰：「可以死矣。」沙門既證聖果，心夷生死，雖入鑊湯，若在清池，有大蓮花而為之座。獄主驚駭，馳使白王，王遂躬觀，深讚靈祐。獄主曰：「大王當死。」王曰：「何。」對曰：「王先垂命，令監刑獄，凡至獄垣皆從殺害，不云王入而獨免死。」王曰：「法已一定，理無再變。我先垂令，豈除汝身？汝久濫生，我之咎也。」即命獄卒，投之洪鑪。獄主既死，王乃得出，於是頹牆堙塹，廢獄寬刑。
en_current: To the north of the old palace there is a stone pillar, several tens of feet high, which is the place where King Aśoka (Aśoka; in the language of the Tang, "No Sorrow"; formerly called Ayuwang, which is an error) established a hell. In the one hundredth year after the Nirvana of the Tathāgata Śākya, there was King Aśoka, the great-grandson of King Bimbisāra (Bimbisāra; in the language of the Tang, "Firm Shadow"; formerly called Pinposuo, which is an error). He moved the capital from Rājagṛha to Pāṭaliputra and built an outer wall that encircled the old city. As the years have passed, only the old foundations remain. Of the monasteries, deva temples, and stūpas, there are several hundred remaining sites, but only two or three still exist. Only to the north of the old palace, bordering the Ganges (Gaṅgā) river, is a small city containing over a thousand families.  Initially, after King Aśoka succeeded to the throne, his conduct was harsh and tyrannical; he established a hell to harm living beings. Lofty walls rose steeply on all sides, with watchtowers standing tall at the corners; there were furnaces of fierce fire and sharp-edged weapons, and all manner of torture instruments were prepared in imitation of the underworld, while a savage man was recruited to be the jailer. At first, criminals from the country who had broken the law were all cast into this pit of fire, regardless of the severity of their offenses. Later, anyone who happened to pass by the prison was seized and executed; all who arrived there died, and thus the evidence was destroyed. At that time, there was a śramaṇa who had newly joined the monastic order; while making his rounds in the neighborhood to beg for food, he happened upon the gate of the prison, and the cruel jailer seized him, intending to do him harm. The śramaṇa was terrified and requested permission to perform repentance. Suddenly, he saw a man brought in bound, his hands and feet severed, his body torn apart; in the blink of an eye, his limbs were scattered and pulverized. Having seen this, the śramaṇa was filled with deep sorrow and pity, cultivated the contemplation of impermanence, and attained the fruit of the arhat (無學果). The jailer said, "You may die now." Having attained the holy fruit, the śramaṇa’s mind was indifferent to life and death; although he was cast into a boiling cauldron, it felt as if he were in a clear pool, with a great lotus flower serving as his seat. The prison warden was terrified and sent a messenger to inform the King. The King then came in person to observe and deeply praised this miraculous protection. The warden said, "Your Majesty must die." The King asked, "Why?" He replied, "Your Majesty previously issued a decree ordering me to oversee the prison, stating that all who reach the prison walls are to be executed, and it did not say that if the King enters, he alone should be exempt from death." The King said, "The law has already been fixed, and the principle cannot be changed again. I issued the order first; how could it exclude you? That you have lived in vain for so long is my fault." He immediately ordered the jailer to throw him into the great furnace. Once the warden was dead, the King was able to leave; he then demolished the walls, filled in the moats, abolished the prison, and lightened the punishments.

zh: 精舍中有大石，如來所履，雙迹猶存，其長尺有八寸，廣餘六寸矣。兩迹俱有輪相，十指皆帶花文，魚形映起，光明時照。昔者如來將取寂滅，北趣拘尸那城，南顧摩揭陀國，蹈此石上，告阿難曰：「吾今最後留此足迹，將入寂滅，顧摩揭陀也。百歲之後，有無憂王命世君臨，建都此地，匡護三寶，役使百神。」及無憂王之嗣位也，遷都築邑，掩周迹石，既近宮城，恒親供養。後諸國王競欲舉歸，石雖不大，眾莫能轉。近者設賞迦王毀壞佛法，遂即石所，欲滅聖迹，鑿已還平，文彩如故，於是捐棄殑伽河流，尋復本處。
en_current: Within the monastery there is a large stone where the Tathāgata (如來) once stepped, and his twin footprints still remain. They are one foot eight inches long and over six inches wide. Both footprints possess the marks of the wheel, the ten toes are all adorned with floral patterns, and the shape of a fish is reflected upon them, shining with light from time to time. In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to attain parinirvāṇa, he headed north toward the city of Kuśinagara (拘尸那城) and looked back south toward the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國). He stepped upon this stone and said to Ānanda, "I now leave these final footprints here as I am about to enter parinirvāṇa, looking back at Magadha. One hundred years hence, there will be a King Aśoka (無憂王) who will rule the world and ascend the throne; he will establish his capital in this place, protect the Three Jewels, and command the hundred spirits." When King Aśoka succeeded to the throne, he moved the capital and built a city, enclosing the stone with the footprints; as it was near the palace, he constantly made offerings to it in person. Later, various kings vied to carry it away, but although the stone was not large, no one was able to move it. Recently, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) destroyed the Buddha-dharma and went to the site of the stone, intending to obliterate the holy relic. After he chiseled it, the surface became smooth again and the patterns remained as before; he then threw it into the Gaṅgā (殑伽河) River, but it soon returned to its original place.

zh: 故宮北有大石室，外若崇山，內廣數丈，是無憂王為出家弟役使神鬼之所建也。初，無憂王有同母弟，名摩醯因陀羅（唐言大帝）。生自貴族，服僣王制，奢侈縱暴，眾庶懷怨。國輔老臣進諫王曰：「驕弟作威，亦已太甚。夫政平則國治，人和則主安，古之則訓，由來久矣。願存國典，收付執法。」無憂王泣謂弟曰：「吾承基緒，覆燾生靈，況爾同胞，豈忘惠愛！不先匡導，已陷刑法。上懼先靈，下迫眾議。」摩醯因陀羅稽首謝曰：「不自謹行，敢干國憲，願賜再生，更寬七日。」於是置諸幽室，嚴加守衛，珍羞上饌，進奉無虧。守者唱曰：「已過一日，餘有六日。」至第六日已，既深憂懼，更勵身心，便獲果證，昇虛空，示神迹，尋出塵俗，遠棲巖谷。無憂王躬往謂曰：「昔拘國制，欲致嚴刑。豈意清昇，取證聖果。既無滯累，可以還國。」弟曰：「昔羈愛網，心馳聲色，今出危城，志悅山谷。願棄人間，長從丘壑。」王曰：「欲靜心慮，豈必幽巖？吾從爾志，當為崇樹。」遂召命鬼神而告之曰：「吾於後日廣備珍羞，爾曹相率來集我會，各持大石，自為床座。」諸神受命，至期畢萃。眾會既已，王告神曰：「石座從橫，宜自積聚。因功不勞，壘為虛室。」諸神受命，不日而成。無憂王躬往迎請，止此山廬。
en_current: To the north of the old palace is a large stone chamber; from the outside it appears like a high mountain, and inside it is several *zhang* wide. It was built by King Aśoka (無憂王) for his younger brother who had left home to become a monk, by employing spirits and ghosts. Originally, King Aśoka had a younger brother by the same mother named Mahendra (摩醯因陀羅; in the language of Tang, "Great Emperor"). Born into the nobility, he wore clothing that usurped royal regulations and was extravagant, indulgent, and violent, causing the populace to harbor resentment. The senior ministers of the state exhorted the king, saying, "Your arrogant brother’s abuse of power has indeed become excessive. When government is equitable, the state is well-ordered; when the people are harmonious, the ruler is secure. This is an ancient teaching that has existed for a long time. We pray you uphold the national laws and hand him over to the law enforcement officials."  King Aśoka said to his brother with tears, "I have inherited the foundation of the ancestors and provide shelter to all living beings; as you are my own flesh and blood, how could I ever forget my kindness and love for you! But because I did not guide you earlier, you have already fallen into the trap of the penal code. Above, I fear the ancestral spirits; below, I am pressured by the public consensus." Mahendra bowed his head and apologized, saying, "I was not prudent in my conduct and dared to violate the national laws; I pray you grant me a new lease on life by allowing a seven-day respite."  Thereupon, he was placed in a secluded chamber and guarded strictly, with fine delicacies and superior food served to him without fail. The guard would call out, "One day has passed; six days remain." By the end of the sixth day, having become deeply fearful and anxious, he exerted his body and mind, attained the fruit of realization, ascended into the void, and manifested miraculous signs. He then departed from the mundane world and dwelt far away in the rocky valleys. King Aśoka went to him in person and said, "Formerly, I was bound by the laws of the state and wished to impose a severe punishment." "How unexpected that you have ascended to purity and attained the holy fruit. Now that you are without attachments or burdens, you may return to the kingdom." The younger brother said, "Formerly I was bound by the net of desire, my mind racing after sounds and forms; now that I have escaped the city of perils, my will finds joy in the mountains and valleys. I wish to abandon the human world and dwell forever among the hills and ravines." The king said, "To quiet the mind and thoughts, is it necessary to seek a secluded cliff? I will follow your wishes and build a retreat for you." He then summoned the spirits and deities and told them, "On a coming day I shall prepare a grand feast of delicacies; you shall lead one another to gather at my assembly, each bringing a large stone to serve as your own seat." The spirits and deities received the order and, when the time arrived, they all gathered. When the assembly had ended, the king said to the spirits, "The stone seats are scattered about; you should stack them up yourselves. With little effort, pile them into a hollow chamber." The spirits and deities received the order and completed it in no time. King Aśoka (無憂王) went in person to welcome and invite him to dwell in this mountain hut.

zh: 故宮西南有小石山，周巖谷間，數十石室，無憂王為近護等諸阿羅漢，役使鬼神之所建立。傍有故臺，餘基積石；
en_current: To the southwest of the old palace is a small rocky hill; among its surrounding cliffs and valleys are several dozen stone chambers, which King Aśoka (無憂王) had built by commanding spirits and deities for the use of Upagupta (近護) and other arhats. Nearby is an ancient terrace, its remaining foundation consisting of a pile of stones.

zh: 池沼漣漪，清瀾澄鑒，隣國遠人謂之聖水，若有飲濯，罪垢消滅。
en_current: The ripples of the pond are clear and reflective like a mirror; people from neighboring countries and distant lands call it holy water, believing that if one drinks from or bathes in it, their sins and impurities will be eliminated.

zh: 山西南有五窣堵波，崇基已陷，餘址尚高，遠而望之，欝若山阜，面各數百步，後人於上重更修建小窣堵波。《印度記》曰：「昔無憂王建八萬四千窣堵波已，尚餘五斗舍利，故別崇建五窣堵波，制奇諸處，靈異間起，以表如來五分法身。薄信之徒竊相評議，云是昔者難陀王建此藏，以儲七寶。其後有王，不甚淳信，聞先疑議，肆其貪求，興動軍師，躬臨發掘，地震山傾，雲昏日翳，窣堵波中大聲雷震，士卒僵仆，象馬驚奔。自茲已降，無敢覬覦。」或曰：「眾議雖多，未為確論；循古所記，信得其實。」
en_current: To the southwest of the mountain are five stūpas. Their lofty foundations have already subsided, yet the remaining sites are still high; viewed from afar, they appear like lush mounds, each side measuring several hundred paces, and people of later generations have built small stūpas atop them. The *Record of India* (Yindu ji 印度記) states: "In the past, after King Aśoka (Wuyou wang 無憂王) had built eighty-four thousand stūpas, there remained five *dou* of relics; therefore, he specially constructed these five stūpas, their design surpassing all other places, where miracles occur from time to time to represent the fivefold Dharma-body (pañca-dharma-kāya 五分法身) of the Tathāgata. Those of shallow faith secretly discussed among themselves, saying that it was King Nanda (Nantuo wang 難陀王) who built this treasury in the past to store his seven treasures. Later, there was a king who was not very devout; hearing these previous rumors, he gave rein to his greed, mobilized his army, and personally oversaw the excavation. The earth quaked and mountains toppled, clouds darkened the sun, a thunderous roar erupted from within the stūpa, soldiers fell prostrate, and elephants and horses fled in terror. From that time on, no one has dared to covet them." Some say: "Although there are many public opinions, they do not constitute a definitive conclusion; by following the ancient records, one can obtain the truth."

zh: 故城東南有屈（居勿反）吒阿濫摩（唐言鷄園）僧伽藍，無憂王之所建焉。無憂王初信佛法也，式遵崇建，修殖善種，召集千僧，凡、聖兩眾，四事供養，什物周給。頹毀已久，基址尚在。伽藍側有大窣堵波，名阿摩落伽者。印度藥果之名也。無憂王搆疾彌留，知命不濟，欲捨珍寶，崇樹福田。權臣執政，誡勿從欲。其後因食，留阿摩落果，玩之半爛，握果長息，問諸臣曰：「贍部洲主今是何人？」諸臣對曰：「唯獨大王。」王曰：「不然。我今非主。唯此半果，而得自在。嗟乎！世間富貴，危甚風燭。位據區宇，名高稱謂，臨終匱乏，見逼強臣，天下非己，半果斯在！」乃命侍臣而告之曰：「持此半果，詣彼雞園，施諸眾僧，作如是說：『昔一贍部洲主，今半阿摩落王，稽首大德僧前，願受最後之施。凡諸所有，皆已喪失，唯斯半果，得少自在。哀愍貧乏，增長福種。』」僧中上座作如是言：「無憂大王宿期弘濟，瘧疾在躬，姦臣擅命，積寶非己，半果為施。承王來命，普施眾僧。」即召典事，羹中總煮。收其果核，起窣堵波。既荷厚恩，遂旌顧命。阿摩落伽窣堵波西北，故伽藍中有窣堵波，謂建揵稚聲。初，此城內伽藍百數，僧徒肅穆，學業清高，外道學人，銷聲緘口。其後僧徒相次徂落，而諸後進莫繼前修。外道師資傅訓成藝，於是命儔召侶，千計萬數，來集僧坊，揚言唱曰：「夫擊揵稚，招集學人！」群愚同止，謬有扣擊。遂白王，請挍優劣。外道諸師高才達學，僧徒雖眾，辭論膚淺。外道曰：「我論勝。自今已後，諸僧伽藍不得擊揵稚以集眾也。」王允其請，依先論制。僧徒受恥，忍詬而退，十二年間不擊揵稚。時南印度那伽閼剌樹那菩薩（唐言龍猛。舊譯曰龍樹，非也），幼傳雅譽，長擅高名，捨離欲愛，出家修學，深究妙理，位登初地。有大弟子提婆者，智慧明敏，機神警悟，白其師曰：「波吒釐城諸學人等辭屈外道，不擊揵稚，日月驟移，十二年矣。敢欲摧邪見山，然正法炬。」龍猛曰：「波吒釐城外道博學，爾非其儔，吾今行矣。」提婆曰：「欲摧腐草，詎必傾山？敢承指誨，黜諸異學。大師立外道義，而我隨文破析，詳其優劣，然後圖行。」龍猛乃扶立外義，提婆隨破其理，七日之後，龍猛失宗，已而歎曰：「謬辭易失，邪義難扶。爾其行矣，摧彼必矣！」提婆菩薩夙擅高名，波吒釐城外道之聞也，即相召集，馳白王曰：「大王昔紆聽覽，制諸沙門不擊揵稚。願垂告命。令諸門候，隣境異僧勿使入城，恐相黨援，輕改先制。」王允其言，嚴加伺候。提婆既至，不得入城。聞其制令，便易衣服，疊僧加胝，置草束中，褰裳疾驅，負戴而入。既至城中，棄草披衣，至此伽藍，欲求止息。知人既寡，莫有相舍，遂宿揵稚臺上。於晨朝時，便大振擊。眾聞伺察，乃客遊比丘。諸僧伽藍傳聲響應。王聞究問，莫得其先，至此伽藍，咸推提婆。提婆曰：「夫揵稚者，擊以集眾。有而不用，懸之何為？」王人報曰：「先時僧眾論議墮負，制之不擊，已十二年。」提婆曰：「有是乎？吾於今日，重聲法鼓。」使報王曰：「有異沙門欲雪前恥。」王乃召集學人，而定制曰：「論失本宗，殺身以謝。」於是外道競陳旗鼓，諠談異義，各曜辭鋒。提婆菩薩既昇論座，聽其先說，隨義析破，曾不浹辰，摧諸異道。國王大臣莫不慶悅，建此靈基，以旌至德。建擊揵稚窣堵波北有故基，昔鬼辯婆羅門所居處也。初，此城中有婆羅門，葺宇荒藪，不交世路，祠鬼求福，魍魎相依。高論劇談，雅辭響應，人或激難，垂帷以對。舊學高才，無出其右，士庶翕然，仰之猶聖。有阿濕縛窶沙（唐言馬鳴）菩薩者，智周萬物，道播三乘，每謂人曰：「此婆羅門學不師受，藝無稽古，屏居幽寂，獨擅高名，將非神鬼相依，妖魅所附，何能若是者乎？夫辯資鬼授，言不對人，辭說一聞，莫能再述，吾今往彼，觀其舉措。」遂即其廬，而謂之曰：「仰欽盛德，為日已久。幸願褰帷，敢申宿志。」而婆羅門居然簡傲，垂帷以對，終不面談。馬鳴心知鬼魅，情甚自負，辭畢而退，謂諸人曰：「吾已知矣，摧彼必矣。」尋往白王：「唯願垂許，與彼居士較論劇談。」王聞駭曰：「斯何人哉！若不證三明，具六通，何能與彼論乎？」命駕躬臨，詳鑒辯論。是時馬鳴論三藏微言，述五明大義，妙辯縱橫，高論清遠。而婆羅門既述辭已，馬鳴重曰：「失吾旨矣，宜重述之。」時婆羅門默然杜口，馬鳴叱曰：「何不釋難？所事鬼魅宜速授辭！」疾褰其帷，視占其怪。婆羅門惶遽而曰：「止！止！」馬鳴退而言曰：「此子今晨聲問失墜，虛名非久，斯之謂也。」王曰：「非夫盛德，誰鑒左道？知人之哲，絕後光前，國有常典，宜旌茂實。」
en_current: To the southeast of the old city is the Kukkuṭārāma (屈吒阿濫摩; 屈 read with the initial of 居 and the final of 勿; in the language of the Tang, "Rooster Garden" [鷄園]) monastery; it was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). When King Aśoka first gained faith in the Buddha-dharma, he followed the teachings to build this monastery and cultivate the seeds of merit; he summoned a thousand monks, both ordinary and holy, providing them with the four requisites and a complete supply of daily necessities. It has long been in ruins, but the foundations still remain. Beside the monastery is a large stūpa named Āmalaka. This is the name of a medicinal fruit in India. King Aśoka fell ill and was on the verge of death; knowing his life could not be saved, he wished to give away his treasures to cultivate a field of merit. However, powerful ministers held the reins of government and warned him not to follow his desires. Later, during a meal, he kept an āmalaka fruit and toyed with it until it was half-rotten; then, clutching the fruit and sighing deeply, he asked his ministers, "Who is now the lord of Jambudvīpa?" The ministers replied, "Only the Great King." The King said, "That is not so. I am no longer the lord. Only this half-fruit is under my control. Alas! The wealth and honor of the world are more precarious than a candle in the wind. Though I occupy the realm and hold a high title, at the end of my life I am destitute, constrained by powerful ministers. The world is no longer mine; only this half-fruit remains!" He then commanded an attendant, saying, "Take this half-fruit to that Rooster Garden, offer it to the assembly of monks, and speak these words: 'The former lord of Jambudvīpa, now the king of half an āmalaka fruit, bows his head before the monks of great virtue and prays that you will accept his final offering. All that I possessed has been lost; only this half-fruit remains, over which I have a little freedom. May you have compassion for the destitute and increase the seeds of merit." The senior monk of the assembly spoke thus: "King Aśoka (無憂大王) long cherished the vow of universal salvation, but now he is afflicted by illness, treacherous ministers have usurped his authority, and the accumulated treasures are no longer his; he offers this half-fruit as alms. We have received the King’s command to distribute it to the entire assembly of monks." He then summoned the steward to boil it all in the soup. They collected the fruit’s pit and erected a stupa. Having received this great kindness, they honored his final request.  To the northwest of the Āmalaka Stupa (阿摩落伽窣堵波), in an old monastery, there is a stupa called "Sound of Striking the Ghaṇṭā" (建揵稚聲). Formerly, there were hundreds of monasteries within this city; the monks were solemn and respectful, their academic pursuits were lofty and pure, and the non-Buddhist scholars kept silent and held their tongues. Later, the monks passed away one after another, and the younger generation failed to continue the practices of their predecessors. The non-Buddhist teachers and disciples passed down their training until they had mastered their arts; they then summoned their companions by the thousands and tens of thousands to assemble at the monastery, shouting aloud: "Strike the ghaṇṭā (揵稚) to summon the scholars!" The ignorant crowd joined in, and they mistakenly struck it. They then reported to the King, requesting a debate to determine who was superior. The non-Buddhist masters were of high talent and great learning, while the monks, though numerous, were shallow in their arguments and discourse. The non-Buddhists said, "Our arguments have prevailed. From this day forward, no monastery shall strike the ghaṇṭā to assemble its members." The King granted their request and issued a decree based on the previous debate. The community of monks, having suffered this shame, endured the insults and withdrew, and for twelve years they did not strike the ghaṇṭā. At that time, in Southern India, there was the Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna (那伽閼剌樹那; in the language of the Tang, Longmeng [龍猛, "Dragon-Valiant"]; the old translation Longshu [龍樹, "Dragon-Tree"] is wrong), who from his youth was renowned for his elegance and in his maturity possessed a great reputation. He abandoned desire and attachment, left the household life to cultivate learning, deeply investigated the subtle principles, and attained the stage of the first bhūmi. He had a great disciple named Deva, who was wise, bright, and quick-witted, with a sharp and alert mind. He said to his teacher, "The scholars of the city of Pāṭaliputra have been defeated in debate by the non-Buddhists and have not struck the ghaṇṭā; time has passed swiftly, and it has been twelve years. I dare to wish to crush the mountain of wrong views and light the torch of the true Dharma." Nāgārjuna said, "The non-Buddhists of Pāṭaliputra are erudite, and you are no match for them; I shall go myself." Deva said, "To crush rotten grass, why must one overturn a mountain? I dare to accept your instruction to dismiss these heterodox teachings. May the Master establish the arguments of the non-Buddhists, and I shall refute them point by point; let us examine their strengths and weaknesses, and then I shall plan my journey." Nāgārjuna then upheld the non-Buddhist arguments, and Deva proceeded to refute his logic. After seven days, Nāgārjuna lost his position, and he sighed, saying, "Fallacious words are easily defeated, and false doctrines are difficult to maintain. You may go now; you will certainly crush them!" Bodhisattva Deva had long enjoyed a great reputation; when the non-Buddhists of Pāṭaliputra heard of him, they immediately assembled and hurried to inform the King, saying, "Your Majesty previously condescended to listen to us and prohibited the monks from striking the ghaṇṭā. We pray that you will issue a decree." "Order the gatekeepers not to allow any strange monks from neighboring territories to enter the city, for fear that they might form a faction and recklessly overturn the previous regulation." The King agreed to their request and strictly increased the surveillance. When Deva (提婆) arrived, he was unable to enter the city. Hearing of the restrictive order, he changed his clothes, folded his saṃghāṭī (僧加胝) robe and placed it inside a bundle of straw, then lifting his skirts and hurrying along, he entered while carrying the bundle on his head. Once inside the city, he discarded the straw and put on his robe, then came to this monastery (saṃghārāma) seeking a place to rest. As he knew few people and no one would offer him lodging, he spent the night on the ghaṇṭā (揵稚) platform. At dawn, he struck it loudly. When the crowd heard it and investigated, they found it was a traveling bhikṣu. All the monasteries echoed the sound in response. When the King heard of this and made inquiries, he could not find the culprit until he reached this monastery, where everyone pointed to Deva. Deva said, "The ghaṇṭā is struck to assemble the community. If one has it but does not use it, why hang it up?" The King’s men replied, "In the past, the monastic community lost a debate, and it was decreed that it should not be struck; it has been twelve years." Deva said, "Is that so? Today, I shall sound the Dharma-drum once more." He sent word to the King, saying, "A strange śramaṇa wishes to wash away the previous shame." The King then summoned the scholars and established a decree, saying, "Whoever loses the debate and abandons their original school shall forfeit their life as an apology." Thereupon, the non-Buddhists vied to display their banners and drums, clamoring with their divergent doctrines, each showing off the sharpness of their rhetoric. Once the Bodhisattva Deva had ascended the debate seat, he listened to the other side speak first, then analyzed and refuted their arguments point by point. In less than twelve days, he had crushed all the heterodox schools. The king and his ministers were filled with joy and built this spiritual foundation to commemorate his supreme virtue. To the north of the stūpa of striking the ghaṇṭā (建擊揵稚窣堵波) is an old foundation, which was formerly the dwelling place of the "Demon-Eloquent Brahman."  Formerly, there was a Brahman in this city who built a hut in a desolate thicket, withdrew from the world, worshipped spirits to seek blessings, and consorted with demons. He engaged in profound discussions and intense debates, his elegant words responding to all inquiries; when people challenged him, he would answer from behind a lowered curtain. Among the scholars and men of talent of that time, none could surpass him, and the gentry and commoners alike looked up to him as if he were a sage.  There was a Bodhisattva named Aśvaghoṣa (阿濕縛窶沙; in the language of the Tang, "Horse-neighing" [馬鳴]), whose wisdom encompassed all things and whose teachings spread through the Three Vehicles. He often said to others, "This Brahman has no teacher for his learning and no ancient precedent for his arts; yet, living in seclusion and solitude, he enjoys a high reputation all to himself. If he were not reliant on ghosts and spirits or possessed by demons, how could he be thus? When eloquence is granted by demons, one cannot speak face-to-face with others, and once their words are heard, they can never be repeated. I shall now go there to observe his conduct."  He then went to the Brahman’s hut and said to him, "I have long admired your great virtue. I hope you will be willing to raise the curtain, as I dare to express a long-held wish." Yet the Brahman remained arrogant and haughty, responding from behind the lowered curtain and refusing to speak face-to-face. Aśvaghoṣa (馬鳴) knew in his heart that it was a demon, yet he was very confident. After taking his leave and withdrawing, he said to the people, "I have already understood it; I shall certainly defeat him." He then went to inform the king, "I only hope you will grant me permission to engage that householder in a rigorous debate." Hearing this, the king was alarmed and said, "What kind of person is this! If one has not realized the three knowledges (三明) and acquired the six supernatural powers (六通), how can one debate with him?" The king ordered his carriage to attend in person to observe the debate in detail. At that time, Aśvaghoṣa discussed the subtle words of the Tripitaka (三藏) and expounded the great principles of the five sciences (五明); his marvelous eloquence was unrestrained, and his lofty arguments were profound and far-reaching. After the Brahman had finished stating his case, Aśvaghoṣa spoke again, saying, "You have missed the gist of my argument; you should state it again." At that moment, the Brahman remained silent and kept his mouth shut. Aśvaghoṣa scolded him, saying, "Why do you not resolve the difficulty? The demon you serve should quickly provide you with words!" He then swiftly lifted the curtain to look at and observe the strange creature. The Brahman was terrified and said, "Stop! Stop!" Aśvaghoṣa withdrew and said, "This fellow’s reputation has collapsed this morning; a false name does not last long—this is what is meant by that." The king said, "If not for a man of great virtue, who could discern the heterodox path? Such wisdom in knowing men is unparalleled in the past and future; the country has established laws, and we should honor such genuine substance."

zh: 城西南隅二百餘里，有伽藍餘跡。其傍有窣堵波，神光時燭，靈瑞間發，近遠眾庶莫不祈請，是過去四佛坐及經行遺迹之所。
en_current: More than two hundred *li* to the southwest of the city, there are the remains of a monastery. Beside it is a *stūpa* where divine light occasionally shines and miraculous signs appear from time to time; the masses, both near and far, never fail to offer their prayers there, for it is the site of the traces where the four past Buddhas sat and performed walking meditation.

zh: 故伽藍西南行百餘里，至鞮羅釋迦伽藍。庭宇四院，觀閣三層，崇臺累仞，重門洞啟，頻毘娑羅王末孫之所建也。旌召高才，廣延俊德，異域學人，遠方髦彥，同類相趨，肩隨戾止。僧徒千數，並學大乘。中門當塗，有三精舍，上置輪相，鈴鐸虛懸，下建層基，軒檻周列，戶牖棟梁，壖垣階陛，金銅隱起，廁間莊嚴。中精舍佛立像高三丈，左多羅菩薩像，右觀自在菩薩像。凡斯三像，鍮石鑄成，威神肅然，冥鑒遠矣。精舍中各有舍利一升，靈光或照，奇瑞間起。
en_current: Traveling southwest from the aforementioned monastery for more than one hundred *li*, one arrives at the Tiladhaka Monastery (鞮羅釋迦伽藍). Its courtyards comprise four precincts, with pavilions and towers of three stories; the elevated terraces rise to a height of many *ren*, and the heavy gates open wide. It was built by a late descendant of King Bimbisāra (頻毘娑羅王). It summons those of high talent and extends a broad invitation to those of eminent virtue; scholars from foreign lands and elites from distant regions, being of the same inclination, flock together, arriving one after another. The community of monks numbers in the thousands, all of whom study the Great Vehicle. Facing the path at the middle gate are three *vihāras* (精舍), topped with wheel-symbols and hung with bells that sway in the air. Below, they are built on tiered foundations with railings surrounding them, while the doors, windows, beams, pillars, walls, and steps are all adorned with inlaid gold and copper reliefs. In the middle *vihāra* is a standing statue of the Buddha thirty feet high, with a statue of Tārā Bodhisattva to the left and a statue of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to the right. All three of these statues are cast from brass; their majestic presence is awe-inspiring, and their spiritual insight reaches far. In each of the *vihāras* there is one *sheng* of relics, which sometimes emit spiritual light and occasionally manifest miraculous omens.

zh: 鞮羅釋迦伽藍西南九十餘里，至大山，雲石幽蔚，靈僊攸舍，毒蛇、暴龍窟穴其藪，猛獸、鷙鳥棲伏其林。山頂有大盤石，上建窣堵波，其高十餘尺，是佛入定處也。昔者如來降神止此，坐斯磐石，入滅盡定，時經宿焉。諸天靈聖供養如來，鼓天樂，雨天花。如來出定，諸天感慕，以寶金銀起窣堵波。去聖逾邈，寶變為石。自古迄今，人未有至。遙望高山，乃見異類，長蛇、猛獸群從右旋，天仙靈聖肩隨讚禮。山東岡有窣堵波，在昔如來佇觀摩揭陀國所履之處也。
en_current: More than ninety *li* southwest of the Tiladhaka Monastery (鞮羅釋迦伽藍), one reaches a great mountain (大山), where the clouds and rocks are dense and secluded, a dwelling place for spirits and immortals; venomous snakes and violent dragons nest in its marshes, and fierce beasts and birds of prey lurk in its forests. On the summit of the mountain is a large flat rock upon which a stūpa over ten feet high is built; this is the place where the Buddha entered into samādhi. In the past, the Tathāgata descended and stayed here, sitting upon this flat rock to enter the cessation samādhi (nirodha-samāpatti) for the duration of one night. The heavenly beings and holy spirits made offerings to the Tathāgata, playing heavenly music and raining down heavenly flowers. When the Tathāgata emerged from samādhi, the heavenly beings, moved by admiration, built a stūpa out of precious gems, gold, and silver. As the time since the Sage’s passing has grown more distant, the precious materials have turned into stone. From ancient times until the present, no human has ever reached it. Looking at the high mountain from afar, one sees strange phenomena: long snakes and fierce beasts circling it to the right in throngs, and heavenly immortals and holy spirits following shoulder to shoulder in praise and worship. On a ridge to the east of the mountain is a stūpa, marking the spot where the Tathāgata once stood gazing at the land of Magadha (摩揭陀國).

zh: 山西北三十餘里，山阿有伽藍，負嶺崇基，疎崖峙閣。僧徒五十餘人，並習大乘法教。瞿那末底（唐言德慧）菩薩伏外道之處。初，此山中有外道摩沓婆者，祖僧佉之法而習道焉。學窮內外，言極空有，名高前列，德重當時。君王珍敬，謂之國寶，臣庶宗仰，咸曰家師。隣國學人承風仰德，儔之先進，誠博達也。食邑二城，環居封建。時南印度德慧菩薩幼而敏達，早擅精微，學通三藏，理窮四諦。聞摩沓婆論極幽微，有懷挫銳，命一門人裁書謂曰：「敬問摩沓婆善安樂也。宜忘勞弊，精習舊學，三年之後，摧汝嘉聲。」如是第二、第三年中，每發使報。及將發迹，重裁書曰：「年期已極，學業何如？吾今至矣，汝宜知之。」摩沓婆甚懷惶懼，誡諸門人及以邑戶：「自今之後，不得居止沙門異道，遞相宣告，勿有犯違。」時德慧菩薩杖錫而來，至摩沓婆邑，人守約，莫有相舍。諸婆羅門更詈之曰：「斷髮殊服，何異人乎？宜時速去，勿此止也！」德慧菩薩欲摧異道，冀宿其邑，因以慈心，卑辭謝曰：「爾曹世諦之淨行，我又勝義諦之淨行，淨行既同，何為見拒？」婆羅門因不與言，但事驅逐。逐出邑外，入大林中。林中猛獸群行為暴，有淨信者恐為獸害，乃束蘊持仗，謂菩薩曰：「南印度有德慧菩薩者，遠傳聲問，欲來論議，故此邑主懼墜嘉聲，重垂嚴制，勿止沙門。恐為物害，故來相援。行矣自安，勿有他慮。」德慧曰：「良告淨信，德慧者，我是也。」淨信聞已，更深恭敬，謂德慧曰：「誠如所告，宜可速行。」即出深林，止息空澤。淨信縱火持弓，周旋左右，夜分已盡，謂德慧曰：「可以行矣，恐人知聞，來相圖害。」德慧謝曰：「不敢忘德。」於是遂行。至王宮，謂門者曰：「今有沙門，自遠而至，願王垂許，與摩沓婆論。」王聞驚曰：「此妄人耳。」即命使臣往摩沓婆所，宣王旨曰：「有異沙門來求談論，今已瑩灑論場，宣告遠近，佇望來儀，願垂降趾。」摩沓婆問王使曰：「豈非南印度德慧論師乎？」曰：「然。」摩沓婆聞，心甚不悅，事難辭免，遂至論場。國王、大臣、士、庶、豪族，咸皆集會，欲聽高談。德慧先立宗義，洎乎景落，摩沓婆辭以年衰，智惛捷對，請歸靜思，方酬來難。每事言歸，及旦昇座，竟無異論。至第六日，歐血而死。其將終也，顧命妻曰：「爾有高才，無忘所恥！」摩沓婆死，匿不發喪，更服鮮綺，來至論會。眾咸諠譁，更相謂曰：「摩沓婆自負才高，恥對德慧，故遣婦來，優劣明矣。」德慧菩薩謂其妻曰：「能制汝者，我已制之。」摩沓婆妻知難而退。王曰：「何言之密，彼便默然？」德慧曰：「惜哉，摩沓婆死矣！其妻欲來與我論耳。」王曰：「何以知之？願垂指告。」德慧曰：「其妻之來也，面有死喪之色，言含哀怨之聲，以故知之，沓婆死矣。能制汝者，謂其夫也。」王命使往觀，果如所議。王乃謝曰：「佛法玄妙，英賢繼軌，無為守道，含識霑化，依先國典，褒德有常。」德慧曰：「苟以愚昧，體道居貞，存正足，論濟物，將弘汲引，先摧傲慢，方便攝化，今其時矣。唯願大王以摩沓婆邑戶子孫千代常充僧伽藍人，則垂誡來葉，流美無窮。唯彼淨信見匡護者福延于世，食用同僧，以勸清信，以褒厚德。」於是建此伽藍，式旌勝迹。初，摩沓婆論敗之後，十數淨行逃難隣國，告諸外道恥辱之事，招募英俊，來雪前恥。王既珍敬德慧，躬往請曰：「今諸外道不自量力，結黨連群，敢聲論鼓，唯願大師摧諸異道。」德慧曰：「宜集論者。」於是外道學人欣然相慰：「我曹今日，勝其必矣。」時諸外道闡揚義理，德慧菩薩曰：「今諸外道逃難遠遊，如王先制，皆是賤人，我今如何與彼對論？」德慧有負座竪，素聞餘論，頗閑微旨，侍立於側，聽諸高談。德慧拊其座而言曰：「床，汝可論。」眾咸驚駭，異其所命。時負座竪便即發難，深義泉涌，清辯響應。三復之後，外道失宗，重挫其銳，再折其翮。自伏論已來，立為伽藍邑戶。
en_current: More than thirty *li* to the northwest of the mountain, in a mountain recess, there is a monastery. It rests against a ridge with a lofty foundation, and its pavilions stand upon sparse cliffs. There are more than fifty monks, all of whom study the teachings of the Mahāyāna. This is the place where the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (瞿那末底; in the language of the Tang, "Virtue-Wisdom" [德慧]) defeated a non-Buddhist.  Formerly, there was a non-Buddhist in this mountain named Mādhava, who took the Sāṃkhya (僧佉) school as his ancestor and practiced its path. His learning exhausted both internal and external doctrines, his words reached the limits of emptiness and existence, his reputation stood above his contemporaries, and his virtue was esteemed at the time. The king cherished and respected him, calling him the "treasure of the country," and the ministers and commoners revered him, all calling him their "family teacher." Scholars from neighboring countries, hearing of his influence and admiring his virtue, ranked him among the foremost, truly a man of broad attainment. He was supported by the income of two cities, which surrounded his residence as a fief.  At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India was quick-witted from his youth; he excelled early in the subtle and profound, his learning mastered the Tripiṭaka, and his reasoning exhausted the Four Noble Truths. Hearing that Mādhava’s theories were extremely profound and subtle, he harbored the intent to blunt his sharp edge. He ordered a disciple to write a letter saying: "I respectfully inquire whether Mādhava is well and at peace. You should forget your weariness and toil, and diligently study your old learning; three years from now, I shall destroy your fine reputation."  In the second and third years, he sent messengers to notify him in this manner. When he was about to set out, he wrote another letter saying: "The time limit has expired; how is your study progressing? I am arriving now; you should be aware of this." Mādhava was filled with great fear and warned his disciples and the inhabitants of his town: "From this day forward, you must not provide lodging to any śramaṇas or followers of heterodox paths; spread this word among yourselves and do not violate this command." At that time, the Bodhisattva Guṇamati (德慧) came carrying his staff and arrived at the town of Mādhava. The people kept their agreement, and no one would offer him lodging. The Brahmins further reviled him, saying, "With your shaven head and strange robes, what strange kind of man are you? You should leave quickly; do not stay here!" The Bodhisattva Guṇamati, wishing to defeat the heterodox teachings and hoping to lodge in the town, spoke with a compassionate heart and humble words, saying, "You all practice the pure conduct of worldly truth, while I practice the pure conduct of the ultimate truth; since our pure conduct is the same, why do you reject me?" The Brahmins would not speak to him, but only sought to drive him away. They drove him out of the town and into a great forest. In the forest, packs of fierce beasts acted with violence. A man of pure faith, fearing he might be harmed by the beasts, bound together a torch and took up a staff, saying to the Bodhisattva, "There is a Bodhisattva Guṇamati of South India whose reputation has spread far and wide, and who intends to come here for a debate; therefore, the lord of this town, fearing the loss of his good name, has strictly decreed that no śramaṇa be allowed to stay. Fearing you might be harmed by the creatures, I have come to assist you. Go now and be at peace; have no other worries." Guṇamati said, "I must tell you, pure believer, that I am Guṇamati." Having heard this, the pure believer showed even deeper respect and said to Guṇamati, "Since it is as you say, you should depart quickly." He then left the deep forest and rested in an empty marsh. The pure believer lit a fire and held his bow, patrolling around him; when the night had ended, he said to Guṇamati, "You may go now, for I fear people may hear of this and come to harm you." Guṇamati thanked him, saying, "I shall not forget your kindness." Thereupon he departed. Arriving at the royal palace, he said to the gatekeeper, "There is a śramaṇa who has come from afar; he requests the king's gracious permission to debate with Mādhava (摩沓婆)." Hearing this, the king was surprised and said, "This is a delusional man." He immediately ordered an envoy to go to Mādhava’s residence to proclaim the royal decree, saying, "An extraordinary śramaṇa has come seeking a debate; the debate hall has now been cleansed and prepared, and an announcement has been sent out far and near; we await your arrival and hope you will grace us with your presence." Mādhava asked the king's envoy, "Is it not the Śāstra Master Guṇamati (德慧) of South India?" The envoy replied, "It is." Upon hearing this, Mādhava was very displeased, but as the matter was difficult to decline, he proceeded to the debate hall. The king, ministers, scholars, commoners, and noble families all gathered to listen to the profound discourse. Guṇamati first established his thesis, and by the time the sun had set, Mādhava excused himself on the grounds of his advanced age and the dullness of his wit in responding quickly, requesting to return home to reflect so that he might respond to the challenge later. Every point was met with a request to return home, and when he ascended the seat the next morning, he ultimately offered no counter-arguments. On the sixth day, he vomited blood and died. As he was about to expire, he looked at his wife and commanded, "You possess great talent; do not forget this shame!" After Mādhava died, his death was concealed and not announced; his wife changed into his fine, colorful robes and came to the debate hall. The crowd broke into a hubbub, saying to one another, "Mādhava is conceited about his own talent and is ashamed to face Guṇamati, so he has sent his wife instead; the difference in their caliber is now clear." Guṇamati Bodhisattva (德慧菩薩) said to his wife, "The one who could control you, I have already subdued." Mādhava’s wife, realizing the difficulty, withdrew. The King asked, "What was that secret conversation, that she became silent?" Guṇamati replied, "Alas, Mādhava is dead! His wife intended to come and debate with me." The King asked, "How did you know this? I wish you would explain it to me." Guṇamati said, "When his wife came, her face bore the look of mourning and her voice was filled with grief and resentment; therefore, I knew that Mādhava was dead. 'The one who could control you' referred to her husband." The King ordered an envoy to go and observe, and it was indeed as discussed. The King then apologized, saying, "The Buddha-Dharma is profound and mysterious; brilliant sages follow in succession. By practicing the Way through non-action, all sentient beings are moistened by its transformation. According to the ancient laws of the state, there is a constant practice of praising virtue." Guṇamati said, "Though I am ignorant, I embody the Way and dwell in purity. If one maintains integrity and seeks to benefit others, then to promote and guide them, one must first crush their arrogance. As for using expedient means to gather and transform them, now is the time. I only wish that Your Majesty would assign the descendants of the households in Mādhava’s fief to serve the monastery (saṃghārāma) for a thousand generations, so as to leave a warning for future ages and spread this beauty boundlessly. And may that man of pure faith who protected me have his blessings extended to his descendants, and may his food and provisions be the same as the monks', so as to encourage the pure-hearted and praise profound virtue." Thereupon, this monastery was built to commemorate this remarkable event. Initially, after Mādhava was defeated in debate, some ten or more Brahmins fled to a neighboring country to escape the disgrace. They reported the humiliation to various heretics (tīrthikas) and recruited talented individuals to come and wash away their previous shame. Since the king esteemed and respected Guṇamati (德慧), he went in person to request him, saying: "Now these heretics, overestimating their own strength, have formed a clique and dared to sound the drum of debate; I only wish that the Great Master would crush these heterodox sects." Guṇamati said: "It is appropriate to assemble the debaters." Thereupon, the heretical scholars comforted one another with joy, saying: "Today, we are certain to be victorious over him." When the heretics began to expound their doctrines, Guṇamati Bodhisattva said: "These heretics fled the disgrace and went far away; according to the king's prior decree, they are all outcasts, so how can I engage in a debate with them?" Guṇamati had a seat-carrier (a servant who carried his portable seat) who had long listened to his debates and was quite familiar with the subtle meanings; he stood by his side, listening to their lofty discourse. Guṇamati patted his seat and said: "Seat, you may debate with them." The assembly was entirely shocked and found his command strange. At that time, the seat-carrier immediately launched his challenge; profound meanings gushed forth like a spring, and his clear eloquence responded to every point. After three rounds, the heretics lost their tenets; their sharpness was severely blunted, and their wings were broken. Ever since they were defeated in debate, they were established as the households of the monastery (saṃghārāma).

zh: 德慧伽藍西南二十餘里，至孤山，有伽藍，尸羅跋陀羅（唐言戒賢）論師論義得勝，捨邑建焉。竦一危峯，如窣堵波，置佛舍利。論師，三摩呾吒國之王族，婆羅門之種也。少好學，有風操，遊諸印度，詢求明哲。至此國那爛陀僧伽藍，遇護法菩薩，聞法信悟。請服染衣，諮以究竟之致，問以解脫之路，既窮至理，亦究微言，名擅當時，聲高異域。南印度有外道，探𦣱索隱，窮幽洞微，聞護法高名，起我慢深嫉，不阻山川，擊鼓求論，曰：「我，南印度之人也。承王國內有大論師，我雖不敏，願與詳議。」王曰：「有之，誠如議也。」乃命使臣請護法曰：「南印度有外道，不遠千里，來求較論，唯願降跡，赴集論場。」護法聞已，攝衣將往。門人戒賢者，後進之翹楚也，前進請曰：「何遽行乎？」護法曰：「自慧日潛暉，傳燈寂照，外道蟻聚，異學蜂飛，故我今者，將摧彼論。」戒賢曰：「恭聞餘論，敢摧異道。」護法知其俊也，因而允焉。是時戒賢年甫三十，眾輕其少，恐難獨任。護法知眾心之不平，乃解之曰：「有貴高明，無云齒歲，以今觀之，破彼必矣。」逮乎集論之日，遠近相趨，少長咸萃。外道弘闡大猷，盡其幽致；戒賢循理責實，深極幽玄。外道辭窮，蒙恥而退。王用酬德，封此邑城。論師辭曰：「染衣之士，事資知足，清淨自守，何以邑為？」王曰：「法王晦迹，智舟淪湑，不有旌別，無勵後學。為弘正法，願垂哀納。」論師辭不獲已，受此邑焉，便建伽藍，窮諸規矩，捨其邑戶，式修供養。
en_current: More than twenty *li* southwest of the Guṇamati (德慧) monastery, one arrives at an isolated hill (孤山). There is a monastery here that was built by the master Śīlabhadra (尸羅跋陀羅) (in the Tang language, Jiexian 戒賢, 'Precept-Worthy') after he won a debate; he donated his village to establish it. A single precipitous peak rises up like a stūpa, and within it are placed relics of the Buddha. The master was of the royal lineage of the country of Samataṭa (三摩呾吒國) and of the Brāhmaṇa caste. In his youth, he was fond of learning and possessed a noble character; he traveled throughout the various regions of India, inquiring after the wise and sagacious. Upon arriving at the Nālandā (那爛陀) monastery in this country, he met the Bodhisattva Dharmapāla (護法), and upon hearing the Dharma, he developed faith and understanding. He requested to don the dyed robes, consulted him on the ultimate goal, and asked about the path to liberation. Having exhausted the highest truths and investigated the subtle words, his fame dominated the era and his reputation was high in foreign lands.  In South India, there was a non-Buddhist who explored the obscure and searched for the hidden, exhausting the profound and penetrating the subtle. Hearing of Dharmapāla’s high fame, he conceived deep arrogance and jealousy, and undeterred by mountains or rivers, he beat the drum to demand a debate, saying: "I am a man of South India. I have heard that there is a great master of debate within this kingdom; although I am not clever, I wish to discuss matters with him in detail." The king said: "It is so; it is truly as you say." He then ordered an envoy to invite Dharmapāla, saying: "A non-Buddhist from South India has come from a distance of a thousand *li* to seek a debate; I only hope you will condescend to attend the assembly at the debate ground." Having heard this, Dharmapāla gathered his robes and prepared to go. His disciple Śīlabhadra, who was the most outstanding among the younger generation, stepped forward and requested: "Why must you go so hastily?" Dharmapāla (護法) said: "Since the Sun of Wisdom has withdrawn its light and the Lamp of the Dharma has ceased its illumination, heretics have gathered like ants and heterodox schools have swarmed like wasps; therefore, I now intend to demolish their arguments." Śīlabhadra (戒賢) said: "I have respectfully heard your arguments; I dare to demolish the heterodox path." Dharmapāla knew that he was a man of outstanding talent and therefore granted his consent. At that time, Śīlabhadra was just thirty years old, and the assembly slighted his youth, fearing he would be unable to shoulder the task alone. Dharmapāla, knowing the dissatisfaction of the assembly, explained to them: "What is valued is brilliance and wisdom, not one's age; from what I see now, he is certain to defeat them."  When the day of the debate arrived, people from far and near flocked to the scene, and both young and old gathered together. The heretic expounded his great principles, exhausting their profound subtleties; Śīlabhadra followed reason to demand the truth, reaching the depths of the abstruse. The heretic’s arguments were exhausted, and he retreated in shame. The king, wishing to reward his virtue, bestowed this city upon him. The Master of Shastras declined, saying: "A man in dyed robes finds his support in contentment and maintains himself in purity; what use has he for a city?" The king said: "The Dharma King has hidden his traces and the Boat of Wisdom has sunk; if there is no recognition, there is nothing to encourage future students. For the sake of propagating the True Dharma, I hope you will compassionately accept it." The Master of Shastras, unable to refuse, accepted the city. He then built a monastery (saṃghārāma), exhausting all the rules of construction, and dedicated the households of the city to provide for its maintenance.

zh: 戒賢伽藍西南行四五十里，渡尼連禪河，至伽耶城。甚險固，少居人，唯婆羅門有千餘家，大仙人祚胤也，王所不臣，眾咸宗敬。城北三十餘里，有清泉，印度相傳謂之聖水，凡有飲濯，罪垢消除。
en_current: Traveling forty or fifty li southwest from the Śīlabhadra Monastery (戒賢伽藍), one crosses the Nairañjanā River (尼連禪河) and reaches the city of Gayā (伽耶城). It is very rugged and well-fortified, but has few inhabitants, except for over a thousand families of Brahmins who are the descendants of a great rishi; the king does not treat them as subjects, and everyone holds them in high esteem. More than thirty li to the north of the city, there is a clear spring which Indian tradition calls holy water; for all who drink from or wash in it, the defilements of sin are eliminated.

zh: 城西南五六里至伽耶山。谿谷杳冥，峯巖危險，印度國俗稱曰靈山，自昔君王馭宇承統，化洽遠人，德隆前代，莫不登封而告成功。山頂上有石窣堵波，高百餘尺，無憂王之所建也，靈鑒潛被，神光時燭，昔如來於此演說《寶雲》等經。伽耶山東南有窣堵波，迦葉波本生邑也。其南有二窣堵波，則伽耶迦葉波、捺地迦葉波（舊曰那提迦葉，訛也。洎諸迦葉，例無波字，略也）事火之處。
en_current: Five or six *li* to the southwest of the city, one arrives at Mount Gayā (伽耶山; Gayā-śīrṣa). The ravines and valleys are dark and deep, and the peaks and cliffs are precipitous. In the customs of the country of India, it is commonly called the Spirit Mountain (靈山). Since ancient times, monarchs who have governed the universe and inherited the succession, whose civilizing influence has reached distant peoples, and whose virtues have surpassed those of previous generations, have all ascended this mountain to perform the *feng* sacrifice and announce their successes. On the summit of the mountain is a stone *stūpa* over one hundred feet high, which was built by King Aśoka (無憂王). Its spiritual efficacy is secretly felt, and divine light occasionally illuminates it; in the past, the Tathāgata expounded the *Ratnamegha* (寶雲) and other sutras here. To the southeast of Mount Gayā is a *stūpa* that marks the native village of Kāśyapa. To its south are two *stūpas*, which are the places where Gayā-Kāśyapa and Nadī-Kāśyapa (formerly called Natijiaye 那提迦葉, which is erroneous; in all the names with Kāśyapa (迦葉) the character 波 (pa) is regularly missing, an abbreviation) practiced fire worship.

zh: 伽耶迦葉波事火東，渡大河，至鉢羅笈菩提山（唐言前正覺山，如來將證正覺，先登此山，故云前正覺也）。如來勤求六歲，未成正覺，後捨苦行，示受乳糜，行自東北，遊目此山，有懷幽寂，欲證正覺。自東北岡登以至頂，地既震動，山又傾搖。山神惶懼，告菩薩曰：「此山者，非成正覺之福地也。若止於此，入金剛定，地當震陷，山亦傾覆。」菩薩下自西南，山半崖中，背巖面㵎，有大石室，菩薩即之，加趺坐焉，地又震動，山復傾搖。時淨居天空中唱曰：「此非如來成正覺處。自此西南十四五里，去苦行處不遠，有卑鉢羅樹，下有金剛座，去來諸佛咸於此座而成正覺，願當就彼。」菩薩方起，室中龍曰：「斯室清勝，可以證聖，唯願慈悲，勿有遺棄。」菩薩既知非取證所，為遂龍意，留影而去（影在昔日，賢愚咸覩：洎於今時，或有得見）。諸天前導，往菩提樹。逮乎無憂王之興也，菩薩登山上下之迹，皆樹旌表，建窣堵波，度量雖殊，靈應莫異，或天花雨空中，或光照幽谷。每歲罷安居日，異方法俗，登修供養，信宿乃還。
en_current: East of the place where Gayā-Kāśyapa worshiped fire, crossing a great river, one reaches the mountain of Prāgbodhi (鉢羅笈菩提山; in the language of Tang, this means "Mountain Prior to Enlightenment"; as the Tathāgata was about to realize perfect enlightenment, he first ascended this mountain, hence it is called "Prior to Enlightenment"). The Tathāgata had sought diligently for six years without attaining perfect enlightenment; he later abandoned austerities and accepted milk gruel. Traveling from the northeast, he gazed upon this mountain and, cherishing its secluded tranquility, desired to realize perfect enlightenment here. He ascended from the northeast ridge to the summit, whereupon the earth quaked and the mountain shook. The mountain god was terrified and told the Bodhisattva, "This mountain is not a blessed place for attaining perfect enlightenment. If you remain here to enter the diamond-like concentration, the earth will quake and collapse, and the mountain will overturn." The Bodhisattva descended from the southwest; halfway down the mountain cliff, with its back to the crags and facing a stream, there was a large stone chamber. The Bodhisattva entered it and sat down cross-legged, whereupon the earth quaked again and the mountain shook once more. At that time, the Pure Abode gods (Śuddhāvāsa-deva) called out from the sky, "This is not the place where the Tathāgata will attain perfect enlightenment. Fourteen or fifteen li to the southwest of here, not far from the place of your austerities, there is a Pippala tree (卑鉢羅樹) with a Diamond Throne beneath it; all Buddhas of the past and future attain perfect enlightenment upon this seat, so we pray you proceed there." Just as the Bodhisattva rose, the dragon of the chamber said, "This chamber is pure and excellent, suitable for realizing the holy state; I only pray that out of compassion, you will not abandon it." The Bodhisattva, knowing that this was not the place to realize enlightenment, in order to fulfill the dragon’s wish, left his shadow behind and departed (The shadow was seen in former days by both the wise and the ignorant; down to the present time, some may still see it). The devas led the way, proceeding to the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹). When King Aśoka (無憂王) rose to power, he erected markers and built stūpas at every spot where the Bodhisattva had ascended or descended the mountain; although these monuments differ in size, their spiritual manifestations are equally remarkable, with celestial flowers sometimes raining from the sky or light illuminating the deep valleys. Every year on the day the summer retreat ends, monks and laypeople from different regions climb the mountain to present offerings, staying for two nights before returning.

zh: 前正覺山西南行十四五里，至菩提樹。周垣壘甎，崇峻險固。東西長，南北狹，周五百餘步。奇樹名花，連陰接影；細沙異草，彌漫綠被。正門東闢，對尼連禪河，南門接大花池，西阨險固，北門通大伽藍。壖垣內地，聖迹相隣，或窣堵波，或復精舍，並贍部洲諸國君王、大臣、豪族欽承遺教，建以記焉。菩提樹垣正中，有金剛座。昔賢劫初成，與大地俱起，據三千大千世界中，下極金輪，上侵地際，金剛所成，周百餘步，賢劫千佛坐之而入金剛定，故曰金剛座焉。證聖道所，亦曰道場，大地震動，獨無傾搖。是故如來將證正覺也，歷此四隅，地皆傾動，後至此處，安靜不傾。自入末劫，正法浸微，沙土彌覆，無復得見。佛涅槃後，諸國君王傳聞佛說金剛座量，遂以兩軀觀自在菩薩像，南北標界，東面而坐。聞諸耆舊曰：「此菩薩像身沒不見，佛法當盡。」今南隅菩薩沒過胸臆矣。金剛座上菩提樹者，即畢鉢羅之樹也。昔佛在世，高數百尺，屢經殘伐，猶高四五丈。佛坐其下成等正覺，因而謂之菩提樹焉。莖幹黃白，枝葉青翠，冬夏不凋，光鮮無變。每至如來涅槃之日，葉皆凋落，頃之復故。是日也，諸國君王，異方法俗，數千萬眾，不召而集，香水香乳，以溉以洗，於是奏音樂，列香花，燈炬繼日，競修供養。如來寂滅之後，無憂王之初嗣位也，信受邪道，毀佛遺迹，興發兵徒，躬臨剪伐。根莖枝葉，分寸斬截，次西數十步而積聚焉，令事火婆羅門燒以祠天，煙焰未靜，忽生兩樹，猛火之中，茂葉含翠，因而謂之灰菩提樹。無憂王覩異悔過，以香乳溉餘根，洎乎將旦，樹生如本。王見靈怪，重深欣慶，躬修供養，樂以忘歸。王妃素信外道，密遣使人，夜分之後，重伐其樹。無憂王旦將禮敬，唯見櫱株，深增悲慨，至誠祈請，香乳溉灌，不日還生。王深敬異，壘石周垣，其高十餘尺，今猶見在。近設賞迦王者，信受外道，毀嫉佛法，壞僧伽藍，伐菩提樹，掘至泉水，不盡根柢，乃縱火焚燒，以甘蔗汁沃之，欲其燋爛，絕滅遺萌。數月後，摩揭陀國補剌拏伐摩王（唐言滿胄），無憂王之末孫也，聞而歎曰：「慧日已隱，唯餘佛樹，今復摧殘，生靈何覩！」舉身投地，哀感動物。以數千牛搆乳而溉，經夜樹生，其高丈餘。恐後剪伐，周峙石垣，高二丈四尺。故今菩提樹隱於石壁，出一丈餘。
en_current: Traveling fourteen or fifteen *li* southwest from the mountain of Prāgbodhi (前正覺山), one arrives at the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹). A surrounding wall of piled bricks is high, steep, and secure. It is long from east to west and narrow from north to south, measuring over five hundred paces in circumference. Rare trees and famous flowers interweave their shade and shadows; fine sand and exotic grasses form a lush, spreading carpet. The main gate opens to the east, facing the Nairañjanā River; the south gate connects to a large flower pond; the west side is closed off and strongly protected; and the north gate leads to a great monastery. Within the enclosure, sacred sites are adjacent to one another, some being stūpas and others being *vihāra*s (精舍). Kings, ministers, and noble families from all the countries of Jambudvīpa, reverently upholding the Buddha’s legacy, have built them as memorials.  In the center of the Mahā-bodhi enclosure is the Vajra Seat (金剛座). Long ago, when the Bhadrakalpa was first formed, it arose together with the great earth. It is situated in the center of the three-thousand great chiliocosm, reaching down to the golden wheel and up to the surface of the ground. It is composed of diamond and measures over a hundred paces in circumference. Because the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa sit upon it to enter the diamond samādhi, it is called the Vajra Seat. It is the place where the holy path is realized, also called the *bodhimaṇḍa* (道場). When the great earth shakes, this place alone does not tremble or sway. For this reason, when the Tathāgata was about to realize perfect enlightenment, he traversed these four corners, and the ground shook everywhere; but when he later arrived at this spot, it was peaceful and did not tilt. Since entering the final age, the True Dharma has gradually faded, and it has become covered with sand and earth, no longer to be seen. After the Buddha’s *nirvāṇa*, kings of various countries, having heard of the dimensions of the Vajra Seat as described by the Buddha, used two statues of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva to mark the northern and southern boundaries, facing toward the east. I have heard from the elders: "When the bodies of these Bodhisattva statues sink and disappear, the Buddha-Dharma will come to an end." Today, the Bodhisattva at the southern corner has sunk past its chest. The Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) on the Vajra Seat is the pippala tree. When the Buddha was in the world, it was several hundred feet high; though it has been repeatedly cut down, it is still four or five zhang high. The Buddha sat beneath it and attained Perfect Enlightenment, and for this reason, it is called the Bodhi tree. Its trunk is yellowish-white, and its branches and leaves are emerald green; they do not wither in winter or summer, and their luster remains unchanged. Every year on the day of the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa*, the leaves all wither and fall, but after a short while, they return to their former state. On that day, the monarchs of various countries, along with clergy and laity from other regions, numbering in the tens of millions, gather without being summoned to water and wash the tree with scented water and milk; they then play music, arrange fragrant flowers, and keep lamps and torches burning day and night, vying with one another to present offerings.  After the Tathāgata’s *nirvāṇa*, when King Aśoka (無憂王) first ascended the throne, he believed in heretical doctrines and destroyed the sacred sites left by the Buddha, mobilizing troops and coming in person to cut the tree down. The roots, stems, branches, and leaves were chopped into small pieces and piled up several dozen paces to the west, where fire-worshiping Brahmins were ordered to burn them as a sacrifice to heaven; yet before the smoke and flames had subsided, two trees suddenly grew out from the midst of the fierce fire with luxuriant, verdant leaves, and were thus called the "Ash Bodhi Trees." King Aśoka witnessed this miracle and repented; he watered the remaining roots with scented milk, and by the time dawn approached, the tree had grown back as it was before. The king witnessed this miracle and was deeply overjoyed; he personally performed offerings, finding such delight that he forgot to return home. The queen, who had long believed in heretical teachings, secretly dispatched messengers after midnight to cut down the tree again. When King Aśoka (無憂王) went to pay his respects at dawn, he saw only a stump; deeply moved by grief, he prayed with utmost sincerity and irrigated it with fragrant milk, and within a few days it grew back to life. The king, deeply respecting this marvel, built a stone wall around it over ten feet high, which can still be seen today.  Recently, King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王), a believer in heretical teachings who slandered and envied the Buddha-dharma, destroyed monasteries and cut down the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree; he dug down to the springs but could not exhaust the roots, so he set it on fire and soaked it with sugarcane juice, wishing to rot it and utterly destroy any remaining sprouts. Several months later, King Pūrṇavarman (補剌拏伐摩王; in Tang language, "Full Armor" [滿胄]) of the kingdom of Magadha (摩揭陀國), the last descendant of King Aśoka, heard of this and sighed, saying: "The sun of wisdom has already set, and only the Buddha-tree remains; now that it has been destroyed again, what will living beings look upon!" He threw his entire body to the ground, his sorrow moving all who saw him. He had the milk of several thousand cows collected to irrigate it, and within a night the tree grew back to a height of over one zhang. Fearing it might be cut down again in the future, he surrounded it with a stone wall twenty-four feet high. Therefore, the Mahā-bodhi tree is now hidden within a stone enclosure, rising more than one zhang above it.

zh: 菩提樹東有精舍，高百六七十尺，下基面廣二十餘步，壘以青甎，塗以石灰，層龕皆有金像，四壁鏤作奇製，或連珠形，或天仙像，上置金銅阿摩落迦果（亦謂寶瓶，又稱寶臺）。東面接為重閣，檐宇特起三層，榱柱棟梁，戶扉寮牖，金銀彫鏤以飾之，珠玉廁錯以填之，奧室邃宇，洞戶三重。外門左右各有龕室，左則觀自在菩薩像，右則慈氏菩薩像，白銀鑄成，高十餘尺。精舍故地，無憂王先建小精舍，後有婆羅門更廣建焉。初，有婆羅門，不信佛法，事大自在天，傳聞天神在雪山中，遂與其弟往求願焉。天曰：「凡諸願求，有福方果。非汝所祈，非我能遂。」婆羅門曰：「修何福可以遂心？」天曰：「欲植善種，求勝福田，菩提樹者，證佛果處也。宜時速反，往菩提樹，建大精舍，穿大水池，興諸供養，所願當遂。」婆羅門受天命，發大信心，相率而返，兄建精舍，弟鑿水池，於是廣修供養，勤求心願，後皆果遂，為王大臣，凡得祿賞，皆入檀捨。精舍既成，招募工人，欲圖如來初成佛像。曠以歲月，無人應召。久之，有婆羅門來告眾曰：「我善圖寫如來妙相。」眾曰：「今將造像，夫何所須？」曰：「香泥耳。宜置精舍之中，并一燈照，我入已，堅閉其戶，六月後乃可開門。」時諸僧眾皆如其命。尚餘四日，未滿六月，眾咸駭異，開以觀之。見精舍內佛像儼然，結加趺坐，右足居上，左手斂，右手垂，東面而坐，肅然如在。座高四尺二寸，廣丈二尺五寸，像高丈一尺五寸，兩膝相去八尺八寸，兩肩六尺二寸，相好具足，慈顏若真，唯右乳上圖瑩未周。既不見人，方驗神鑒，眾咸悲歎，慇懃請知。有一沙門，宿心淳質，乃感夢見往婆羅門而告曰：「我是慈氏菩薩，恐工人之思不測聖容，故我躬來圖寫佛像。垂右手者，昔如來之將證佛果，天魔來嬈，地神告至，其一先出，助佛降魔，如來告曰：『汝勿憂怖，吾以忍力，降彼必矣。』魔王曰：『誰為明證？』如來乃垂手指地，言：『此有證。』是時第二地神踊出作證，故今像手倣昔下垂。」眾知靈鑒，莫不悲感。於是乳上未周，填廁眾寶，珠瓔寶冠，奇珍交飾。設賞迦王伐菩提樹已，欲毀此像，既覩慈顏，心不安忍，迴駕將返，命宰臣曰：「宜除此佛像，置大自在天形。」宰臣受旨，懼而歎曰：「毀佛像則歷劫招殃，違王命乃喪身滅族，進退若此，何所宜行！」乃召信心以為役使，遂於像前橫壘甎壁，心慚冥闇，又置明燈，甎壁之前畫自在天。功成報命，王聞心懼，舉身生皰，肌膚攫裂，居未久之，便喪沒矣。宰臣馳返，毀除障壁，時經多日，燈猶不滅。像今尚在，神工不虧。既處奧室，燈炬相繼，欲覩慈顏，莫由審察，必於晨朝持大明鏡，引光內照，乃覩靈相。夫有見者，自增悲感。如來以印度吠舍佉月後半八日成等正覺，當此三月八日也。上座部則吠舍佉月後半十五日成等正覺，當此三月十五日也。是時如來年三十矣。或曰年三十五矣。菩提樹北有佛經行之處。如來成正覺已，不起于座，七日寂定。其起也，至菩提樹北，七日經行，東西往來，行十餘步，異華隨迹十有八文。後人於此壘甎為基，高餘三尺。聞諸先志曰：此聖迹基，表人命之脩短也，先發誠願，後乃度量，隨壽脩短，數有增減。經行基北，道右，盤石上，大精舍中，有佛像，舉目上望。昔者，如來於此七日觀菩提樹，目不暫捨。為報樹恩，故此瞻望。菩提樹西不遠，大精舍中，有鍮石佛像，飾以奇珍，東面而立。前有青石，奇文異采，是昔如來初成正覺，梵王起七寶堂，帝釋建七寶座，佛於其上七日思惟，放異光明，照菩提樹。去聖悠遠，寶變為石。菩提樹南不遠，有窣堵波，高百餘尺，無憂王之所建也。菩薩既濯尼連河，將趣菩提樹，竊自思念何以為座？尋自發明當須淨草。天帝釋化其身為刈草人，荷而逐路。菩薩謂曰：「所荷之草頗能惠耶？」化人聞命，恭以草奉，菩薩受已，執而前進。受草東北不遠，有窣堵波，是菩薩將證佛果，青雀、群鹿呈祥之處。印度休徵，斯為嘉應，故淨居天隨順世間，群從飛繞，効靈顯聖。菩提樹東，大路左右，各一窣堵波，是魔王嬈菩薩處也。菩薩將證佛果，魔王勸受輪王，策說不行，殷憂而返。魔王之女請往誘焉，菩薩威神，衰變冶容，扶羸策杖，相携而退。菩提樹西北，精舍中，有迦葉波佛像，既稱靈聖，時燭光明。聞諸先記曰：若人至誠，旋繞七周，在所生處，得宿命智。迦葉波佛精舍西北二甎室，各有地神之像。昔者如來將成正覺，一報魔至，一為佛證。後人念功，圖形旌德。菩提樹垣西不遠，有窣堵波，謂欝金香，高四十餘尺，漕炬吒國商主之所建也。昔漕炬吒國有大商主，宗事天神，祠求福利，輕蔑佛法，不信因果。其後將諸商侶，貿遷有無，泛舟南海，遭風失路，波濤飄浪，時經三歲，資糧罄竭，糊口不充。同舟之人，朝不謀夕，勠力同志，念所事天，心慮已勞，冥功不濟。俄見大山，崇崖峻嶺，兩日聯暉，重明照朗。時諸商侶更相慰曰：「我曹有福，過此大山，宜於中止，得安樂。」商主曰：「非山也，乃摩竭魚耳。崇崖峻嶺，鬚鬣也；兩日聯暉，眼光也。」言聲未靜，舟帆飄湊。於是商主告諸侶曰：「我聞觀自在菩薩於諸危厄能施安樂，宜各至誠，稱其名字。」遂即同聲，歸命稱念。崇山既隱，兩日亦沒。俄見沙門，威儀庠序，杖錫凌虛，而來拯溺，不踰時而至本國矣。因即信心貞固，求福不回，建窣堵波，式修供養，以欝金香泥而周塗上下。既發信心，率其同志，躬禮聖迹，觀菩提樹。未暇言歸，已淹晦朔。商侶同遊，更相謂曰：「山川悠間，鄉國遼遠，昔所建立窣堵波者，我曹在此，誰其灑掃？」言訖，旋繞至此，忽見窣堵波，駭其由致，即前瞻察，乃本國所建窣堵波也。故今印度因以欝金為名。菩提樹垣東南隅，尼拘律樹側，窣堵波傍有精舍，中作佛坐像。昔如來初證佛果，大梵天王於此勸請轉妙法輪。菩提樹垣內，四隅皆有大窣堵波。在昔如來受吉祥草已，趣菩提樹，先歷四隅，大地震動，至金剛座，方得安靜。樹垣之內，聖迹鱗次，羌難遍舉。菩提樹垣外，西南窣堵波，奉乳糜二牧女故宅。其側窣堵波，牧女於此煮糜。次此窣堵波，如來受糜處也。菩提樹垣南門外有大池，周七百餘步，清瀾澄鏡，龍魚潛宅，婆羅門兄弟承大自在天命之所鑿也。次南一池，在昔如來初成正覺，方欲浣濯，天帝釋為佛化成池。西有大石，佛浣衣已，方欲曝曬，天帝釋自大雪山持來也。其側窣堵波，如來於此納故衣。次南林中窣堵波，如來受貧老母施故衣處。
en_current: To the east of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is a vihāra (精舍), one hundred and sixty or seventy feet high, with a base more than twenty paces wide, built of blue bricks and plastered with lime. The tiered niches all contain golden images, and the four walls are carved with exquisite designs, some in the form of linked pearls, others as celestial beings. At the top is placed a golden-copper āmalaka fruit (also called a treasure vase, or a treasure terrace). The eastern side is connected to a multi-storied pavilion with eaves and roofs rising in three distinct tiers; the rafters, pillars, beams, doors, and windows are decorated with gold and silver carvings and inlaid with pearls and jade. The inner chambers and deep halls have three sets of connecting doors. On the left and right of the outer gate are niche chambers; on the left is an image of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva (觀自在菩薩), and on the right is an image of Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩), both cast in white silver and over ten feet high. On the original site of the vihāra, King Aśoka (無憂王) first built a small vihāra, which was later expanded by a Brahmin. Initially, there was a Brahmin who did not believe in the Buddha’s teachings and worshipped Maheśvara (大自在天). Hearing that the deity resided in the Snow Mountains, he went there with his younger brother to seek the fulfillment of his vows. The deity said, "All wishes and prayers are fulfilled only when one has merit. What you pray for is not something I can grant." The Brahmin asked, "What merit should I cultivate to fulfill my heart's desire?" The deity replied, "If you wish to plant good seeds and seek a superior field of merit, the Mahā-bodhi is the place where the Buddha attained the fruit of enlightenment. You should return quickly, go to the Mahā-bodhi, build a great vihāra, dig a large water pond, and perform various offerings; then your wishes shall be fulfilled." The Brahmin, having received the divine command, conceived great faith and returned together; the elder brother built a vihāra (精舍) and the younger brother excavated a water pond. Thereupon, they performed grand offerings and diligently sought the fulfillment of their heart’s desires, which were eventually realized as they became high ministers to the king, and all the emoluments and rewards they received were given away as alms. Once the vihāra was completed, they sought to recruit craftsmen to fashion an image of the Tathāgata as he first attained Buddhahood. A long time passed, and no one responded to the call. After a while, a Brahmin came and told the assembly, "I am skilled at depicting the wondrous form of the Tathāgata." The assembly asked, "Now that we are to create the image, what do you require?" He replied, "Only scented clay. It should be placed inside the vihāra, along with a single lamp for illumination. Once I have entered, seal the door firmly; it may only be opened after six months." The monastic assembly followed his instructions. With four days still remaining before the six months were up, the assembly became alarmed and curious, and they opened the door to look inside. They saw the Buddha image inside the vihāra looking majestic, sitting cross-legged with the right foot on top, the left hand withdrawn, and the right hand hanging down, facing east and appearing as solemn as if it were alive. The pedestal was four feet two inches high and twelve feet five inches wide; the image was eleven feet five inches tall, with a distance of eight feet eight inches between the knees and six feet two inches between the shoulders. Its auspicious marks were complete and its compassionate face seemed real, except that the polishing above the right breast was not yet finished. Since the man was nowhere to be seen, they realized it was a divine manifestation, and the assembly sighed with sorrow and earnestly prayed to understand. There was a śramaṇa of simple and honest character who had a dream in which the former brahmin appeared and said to him, "I am Maitreya Bodhisattva (慈氏菩薩); fearing that the thoughts of craftsmen could not fathom the holy countenance, I came in person to depict the Buddha's image. As for the lowered right hand, formerly when the Tathāgata was about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, the celestial Māra came to harass him, and an earth deity announced his arrival. One of them emerged first to help the Buddha subjugate the demon, but the Tathāgata told him, 'Do not be worried or afraid; I shall surely subjugate him through the power of forbearance.' The demon king asked, 'Who will be the clear witness?' The Tathāgata then lowered his hand and pointed to the ground, saying, 'This is the witness.' At that time, the second earth deity emerged to bear witness; therefore, the hand of the present image imitates that former posture of lowering." The assembly, knowing of this spiritual manifestation, was filled with sorrow and reverence. Consequently, where the area above the breast was not yet finished, they filled it with various precious substances, and adorned it with pearl necklaces, jeweled crowns, and rare treasures.  After King Śaśāṅka (設賞迦王) had felled the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) tree, he wished to destroy this image; however, once he beheld its compassionate countenance, his heart could not bear it, and as he turned his carriage to return, he commanded a high minister, saying, "You should remove this Buddha image and install a figure of Maheśvara (大自在天)." Having received the decree, the minister was afraid and sighed, saying, "If I destroy the Buddha image, I shall incur calamity for kalpas to come; yet if I disobey the King's command, I shall lose my life and have my clan exterminated. In such a dilemma, what is the proper course of action!" He then summoned men of faith to serve as laborers and built a brick wall across the front of the image; feeling ashamed that it would be in total darkness, he also placed a bright lamp inside, and on the front of the brick wall, he painted a picture of Maheśvara. When the work was completed, he reported back to the King. Upon hearing this, the King was terrified; his entire body broke out in pustules, his skin and flesh cracked and split, and before long, he died. The minister hurried back and destroyed the wall that had served as a barrier. Although many days had passed, the lamp was still not extinguished. The image remains to this day, and the divine craftsmanship is unimpaired. Since it is situated in a secluded chamber where lamps are kept burning in succession, one who wishes to behold the compassionate countenance cannot examine it clearly; one must hold a large, bright mirror in the morning to reflect light inside, and only then can the sacred image be seen. Those who see it naturally feel an increase in sorrow and reverence.  The Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment on the eighth day of the second half of the Indian month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the eighth day of the third month in our calendar. According to the Sthavira school, however, he attained perfect enlightenment on the fifteenth day of the second half of the month of Vaiśākha, which corresponds to the fifteenth day of the third month. At that time, the Tathāgata was thirty years old; others say he was thirty-five.  To the north of the Mahā-bodhi (菩提樹) is the place where the Buddha walked in meditation. After the Tathāgata attained perfect enlightenment, he did not rise from his seat for seven days, remaining in silent meditation. When he arose, he went to the north of the Mahā-bodhi and walked in meditation for seven days, pacing back and forth from east to west for more than ten paces. Extraordinary flowers appeared in his footprints, numbering eighteen in total. Later generations built a brick foundation here, more than three feet high. I have heard from ancient records that this sacred foundation indicates the length of a person's life: if one first makes a sincere vow and then measures it, the number will increase or decrease according to the length of one's lifespan. To the north of the meditation foundation, on the right side of the path, upon a large rock, there is a great shrine (精舍) containing a Buddha image that is looking upward with its eyes raised. In the past, the Tathāgata spent seven days here gazing at the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹) without once averting his eyes. He did this to repay the tree for its kindness, and thus he kept it in his view. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree, in a great shrine (精舍), there is a brass Buddha image adorned with rare jewels, standing and facing east. In front of it is a blue stone with wonderful patterns and extraordinary colors; this is where, when the Tathāgata first attained perfect enlightenment, the Brahma King (Brahmā) built a hall of seven treasures and Lord Indra (Śakra) constructed a throne of seven treasures, upon which the Buddha meditated for seven days, emitting a wondrous light that illuminated the Mahā-bodhi tree. As the time since the Sage’s passing is long, the treasures have turned into stone.  Not far to the south of the Mahā-bodhi tree, there is a stūpa over a hundred feet high, built by King Aśoka (無憂王). When the Bodhisattva had bathed in the Nairañjanā River and was about to proceed to the Mahā-bodhi tree, he secretly pondered what he should use for a seat. He soon realized that he required clean grass. Lord Indra (天帝釋) transformed himself into a grass-cutter, carrying grass and following the path. The Bodhisattva said to him, "Could you bestow upon me some of the grass you are carrying?" The transformed being, hearing this request, respectfully offered the grass, which the Bodhisattva accepted, holding it as he proceeded forward.  Not far to the northeast of where he received the grass, there is a stūpa, which marks the place where bluebirds and herds of deer presented auspicious omens when the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood. In India, such signs are considered favorable omens; therefore, the gods of the Pure Abodes (Śuddhāvāsa-deva) conformed to the ways of the world, and the flocks followed, flying and circling to manifest their spiritual power and reveal the holiness of the site. To the east of the Mahā-bodhi tree, on either side of the main road, there is a stūpa; these are the places where the King of Māras disturbed the Bodhisattva. When the Bodhisattva was about to attain the fruit of Buddhahood, the King of Māras urged him to accept the position of a Wheel-Turning King; when his entreaties failed, he returned in deep sorrow. The daughters of the King of Māras requested to go and seduce him, but through the Bodhisattva’s divine power, their beautiful appearances withered and changed; they withdrew supporting one another, frail and leaning on staves. To the northwest of the Mahā-bodhi tree (菩提樹), inside a shrine (精舍), there is an image of Kāśyapa Buddha; it is renowned for its spiritual efficacy and frequently emits a brilliant light. According to ancient records, if a person with utmost sincerity circumambulates it seven times, they will attain the knowledge of past lives in whatever place they are reborn. To the northwest of the Kāśyapa Buddha shrine are two brick chambers, each containing an image of an earth deity. In the past, when the Tathāgata was about to attain perfect enlightenment, one reported the arrival of Māra, and the other served as a witness for the Buddha. Later generations, mindful of their service, depicted their forms to honor their virtue. Not far to the west of the Mahā-bodhi tree enclosure, there is a stūpa called the Saffron (郁金香) Stūpa, over forty feet high, which was built by a merchant lord of the country of Jāguḍa (漕炬吒國). Formerly, in the country of Jāguḍa, there was a great merchant lord who worshiped heavenly deities and offered sacrifices to seek blessings, while holding the Buddha’s teachings in contempt and disbelieving in cause and effect.
